items.question_md:
A 10 kVA, 2500/250 V, 1-$\phi$ Transformer gave the following test results:

Open circuit test: 250 V, 0.8 A, 50 W

Short circuit test: 60 V, 4 A, 80 W

Compute the voltage regulation and the secondary terminal voltage under the rated load at 0.8 lagging p.f.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 10 kVA, 2500/250 V. SC (HV): 60 V, 4 A, 80 W; rated HV current $= 10000/2500 = 4$ A. pf $= 0.8$ lag ($\sin\phi = 0.6$).

**Equivalent parameters (HV side):**
$$Z_{01} = \frac{60}{4} = 15\ \Omega, \quad R_{01} = \frac{80}{4^2} = 5\ \Omega, \quad X_{01} = \sqrt{15^2 - 5^2} = 14.14\ \Omega$$

**Regulation:**
$$\%R = \frac{I_1(R_{01}\cos\phi + X_{01}\sin\phi)}{V_1}\times 100 = \frac{4(5 \times 0.8 + 14.14 \times 0.6)}{2500}\times 100 = \frac{49.94}{2500}\times 100$$
$$\boxed{\%R \approx 2.00\%}$$

**Secondary terminal voltage:**
$$V_2 = 250(1 - 0.01998) \approx \mathbf{245.0\ V}$$
(Check on LV side: $R_{02} = 0.05\ \Omega$, $X_{02} = 0.1414\ \Omega$, $I_2 = 40$ A, drop $= 40(0.04 + 0.0849) = 4.99$ V.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the phenomena of P-N junction diode with a neat diagram and differentiate the working of the diode in forward and reverse biasing. Why the Zener diode is always operate in reverse biasing.
items.answer_md:
**Formation of the junction:** when P-type and N-type silicon are joined, holes diffuse from P to N and electrons from N to P, and recombine near the junction. This leaves immobile negative acceptor ions on the P side and positive donor ions on the N side. This region, empty of mobile carriers, is the **depletion layer**. Its electric field sets up a **barrier potential** of about **0.7 V (Si)** or **0.3 V (Ge)**, which stops further diffusion.

*Diagram (in words):* a bar, P on the left with holes (o), N on the right with electrons (•); a narrow central band with − ions on the P side and + ions on the N side, labelled "depletion layer"; the field $E$ points from N to P.

**Forward vs reverse biasing:**

| | Forward bias | Reverse bias |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | P to +, N to − | P to −, N to + |
| Barrier / depletion layer | Reduced, narrows | Increased, widens |
| Current | Large (mA) after cut-in voltage $V_\gamma$ (0.7 V Si) | Tiny reverse saturation current $I_0$ (μA/nA) |
| Carriers responsible | Majority carriers | Minority carriers |
| Resistance | Low (few ohms) | Very high (MΩ) |
| Behaviour | Closed switch | Open switch, until breakdown |

**Why a Zener diode is always operated in reverse bias:**
- In forward bias a Zener behaves like an ordinary diode (about 0.7 V drop), so it has no special use.
- It is heavily doped so that it breaks down sharply at a definite, low reverse voltage $V_Z$ (Zener breakdown).
- In the breakdown region the voltage across it stays almost **constant at $V_Z$** over a wide range of current, and the breakdown is not destructive as long as the power rating is not exceeded.
- This constant voltage is what makes it useful as a **voltage regulator** and reference, so it is connected in reverse bias.

items.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers
items.question_md: Explain the working of the full wave rectifier and drive the expression of output voltage and efficiency of the same.
items.answer_md:
## Full-wave rectifier

**Circuit (centre-tap):** a transformer with a centre-tapped secondary; diode $D_1$ from the top end A and diode $D_2$ from the bottom end B, their cathodes joined at one end of $R_L$; the other end of $R_L$ goes to the centre tap C. Each half of the secondary supplies $V_m\sin\omega t$.

**Working:**
1. **Positive half cycle** (A positive w.r.t. C): $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts; $D_2$ is reverse biased. Current flows A, $D_1$, $R_L$ (top to bottom), C.
2. **Negative half cycle** (B positive w.r.t. C): $D_2$ conducts, $D_1$ is off. Current flows B, $D_2$, $R_L$ (same direction, top to bottom), C.
3. So the load current flows in the **same direction in both half cycles**: the output is a series of positive half-sine humps.
4. The non-conducting diode sees the whole secondary voltage, so **PIV $= 2V_m$** for the centre-tap circuit ($V_m$ for a bridge).

**Waveforms** (drawn one under the other on the same time axis):
- Input: sine wave $V_m\sin\omega t$ with period $T$.
- $i_{D1}$: humps in $0$ to $T/2$ only; $i_{D2}$: humps in $T/2$ to $T$ only.
- Load voltage $v_L$: a hump in every half cycle, peak $V_m$ (less the diode drop), frequency $2f$ = 100 Hz for 50 Hz mains.

**Derivation** (diode resistance $r_f$, load $R_L$, $\theta = \omega t$). In each half cycle one path conducts, so the load current is
$$i = I_m\sin\theta \ \ (0 \le \theta \le \pi), \qquad I_m = \frac{V_m}{r_f + R_L}$$
and the same hump repeats every $\pi$.

*DC (average) current:*
$$I_{dc} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{I_m}{\pi}\big[-\cos\theta\big]_0^{\pi} = \frac{2I_m}{\pi}$$
so $V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = \dfrac{2I_mR_L}{\pi} \approx \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}$ when $r_f \ll R_L$.

*RMS current:*
$$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta} = \sqrt{\frac{I_m^2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}} = \frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$$

*Efficiency:*
$$P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = \frac{4I_m^2}{\pi^2}R_L, \qquad P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(r_f + R_L) = \frac{I_m^2}{2}(r_f + R_L)$$
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{R_L}{r_f + R_L} = \frac{0.812}{1 + r_f/R_L}$$
**Maximum efficiency** (when $r_f \ll R_L$): $\mathbf{\eta_{max} = 81.2\%}$, twice the half-wave value of 40.6%.

**Output voltage:** with ideal diodes, $V_{dc} = \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi} = 0.637V_m$ and $V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt2}$. Ripple factor $\gamma = \sqrt{\pi^2/8 - 1} = 0.482$.

items.question_md:
Calculate the current in 3 ohm resistor using super position theorem.

[Figure: Circuit with four vertical branches connected between a top and bottom rail. Leftmost branch: $10\,\Omega$ resistor in series with a $20\,A$ current source (arrow pointing up). Second branch: $9\,\Omega$ resistor. A $3\,\Omega$ resistor in the top rail between the second and third branches. Third branch: $6\,\Omega$ resistor. A $10\,V$ voltage source (+ on left, − on right) in the top rail between the third branch and the rightmost branch. Rightmost branch: $2\,\Omega$ resistor.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading:** nodes P (top of 20 A branch and 9 Ω), Q (after the 3 Ω, top of 6 Ω) and R (after the 10 V source, top of 2 Ω). The 20 A source (arrow up) is in series with 10 Ω; the 10 V source has + on the Q side, so $V_Q - V_R = 10$ V.

**(i) 20 A alone** (10 V shorted, so Q and R are joined). The 10 Ω in series with the current source has no effect. From P: 9 Ω, and $3 + (6 \parallel 2) = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5\ \Omega$. Current divider:
$$I_3' = 20 \times \frac{9}{9 + 4.5} = 13.33\ \text{A}\ (\text{P to Q})$$

**(ii) 10 V alone** (20 A opened). At Q the source sees 6 Ω in parallel with $(3 + 9) = 12\ \Omega$, i.e. 4 Ω; at R it sees 2 Ω.
$$I = \frac{10}{4 + 2} = 1.667\ \text{A},\quad V_Q = 1.667 \times 4 = 6.667\ \text{V}$$
$$I_3'' = \frac{6.667}{12} = 0.556\ \text{A}\ (\text{Q to P})$$

**Total (P to Q positive):**
$$I_3 = 13.33 - 0.556 = \mathbf{12.78\ A}\ \text{from P to Q}$$

Check (nodal): $V_P = 65$ V, $V_Q = 26.67$ V, $(65 - 26.67)/3 = 12.78$ A.

items.question_md:
With the help of Thevenin's theorem, calculate current flowing through the $3\Omega$ resistor in the network of given figure.

[Figure: Network with left branch containing a $24\,V$ battery in series with a $4\,\Omega$ resistor; top rail has an $8\,\Omega$ resistor followed by another $8\,\Omega$ resistor; middle branch (at node between the two $8\,\Omega$ resistors) contains a $2\,A$ current source (arrow up) in parallel with a $4\,\Omega$ resistor; right branch contains the $3\,\Omega$ resistor; all branches return to a common bottom rail.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 24 V in series with 4 Ω (left branch, node L); 8 Ω from L to middle node M; at M, 2 A source (up) in parallel with 4 Ω; 8 Ω from M to node R; 3 Ω from R to the bottom rail.

**Step 1: Remove the 3 Ω.** No current in the second 8 Ω, so $V_{th} = V_M$.

**Step 2: $V_{th}$.** The 24 V source sees $4 + 8 = 12\ \Omega$ up to M. KCL at M:
$$\frac{V_M - 24}{12} + \frac{V_M}{4} = 2 \Rightarrow V_M\left(\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{4}\right) = 2 + 2 \Rightarrow V_M = \frac{4}{1/3} = 12\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: $R_{th}$** (24 V shorted, 2 A opened):
$$R_{th} = \big[(4 + 8) \parallel 4\big] + 8 = 3 + 8 = 11\ \Omega$$

**Step 4:**
$$I_3 = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + 3} = \frac{12}{14} = \mathbf{0.857\ A}\ \text{(downward)}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the relation between the voltage and current for an R-L-C circuit using phasor diagram. Also derive the average power consumed by the circuit. Define and explain the condition of Series resonance.
items.answer_md:
### Voltage–current relation (phasor diagram)
In a series R-L-C circuit the same current $I$ flows through every element, so $I$ is the reference phasor.
- $V_R = IR$, in phase with $I$.
- $V_L = IX_L$, leading $I$ by 90°, $X_L = 2\pi fL$.
- $V_C = IX_C$, lagging $I$ by 90°, $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}$.

$V_L$ and $V_C$ are in direct opposition, so their net is $(V_L - V_C)$. The supply voltage is the phasor sum (diagram: $V_R$ horizontal, $V_L - V_C$ vertical, $V$ the hypotenuse at angle $\phi$ to $I$):
$$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = IZ$$
$$I = \frac{V}{Z},\quad Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\quad \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$
So if $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, then $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ with $I_m = V_m/Z$: current lags when $X_L > X_C$, leads when $X_C > X_L$.

### Average power
$$p = vi = V_mI_m\sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$
Averaging over one cycle, the $\cos(2\omega t - \phi)$ term gives zero:
$$\boxed{P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\phi = VI\cos\phi = I^2R\ \text{W}},\qquad \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$$

### Series resonance
**Definition:** a series RLC circuit is at resonance when its net reactance is zero, $X_L = X_C$, so the supply voltage and current are in phase.
$$2\pi f_0L = \frac{1}{2\pi f_0C}\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$
**At resonance:**
- $Z = R$ (minimum), so $I_0 = V/R$ (maximum).
- $\phi = 0$, power factor $= 1$, $P = VI = I_0^2R$.
- $V_L = V_C$ and cancel; each may be many times $V$ (voltage magnification, $Q = \dfrac{V_L}{V} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$).
- Below $f_0$ the circuit is capacitive; above $f_0$ it is inductive.

items.question_md:
A coil having both resistance and inductance has a total effective impedance of $50\Omega$ and the phase angle of the current through it with respect to the voltage across it is $45^\circ$ lag. The coil is connected in series with a $40\Omega$ resistor across a sinusoidal supply. The circuit current is 3A. Find (i) supply voltage and (ii) circuit phase angle.

[Figure: Sinusoidal source $V_s$ driving current $I = 3A$ through $R = 40\Omega$ in series with a coil represented by $R_c$ and $L_c$ in series, with $Z_c = 50\Omega$.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** coil $Z_c = 50\ \Omega$ at $45^\circ$ lag; series resistor $R = 40\ \Omega$; $I = 3$ A.

**Coil components**
$$R_c = Z_c\cos45^\circ = 50\times0.7071 = 35.36\ \Omega,\qquad X_c = Z_c\sin45^\circ = 35.36\ \Omega$$

**Total circuit**
$$R_T = 40 + 35.36 = 75.36\ \Omega,\quad X = 35.36\ \Omega$$
$$Z = \sqrt{75.36^2 + 35.36^2} = 83.24\ \Omega$$

**(i) Supply voltage**
$$V_s = IZ = 3\times83.24 = \mathbf{249.7\ V}\ (\approx 250\ \text{V})$$

**(ii) Circuit phase angle**
$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X}{R_T} = \tan^{-1}\frac{35.36}{75.36} = \mathbf{25.14^\circ},\ \text{current lagging}$$
(pf $= \cos25.14^\circ = 0.905$ lagging.)

Phasor check: $V_R = 120$ V in phase with $I$; $V_{coil} = 150$ V at 45° ahead of $I$; their phasor sum is 249.7 V, not $120 + 150 = 270$ V.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: With the help of neat sketches explain the Core type and Shell type transformer. Discuss their advantages and disadvantages. Draw the equivalent circuit diagram and phasor diagram of the transformer for lagging p.f. load.
items.answer_md:
**Core type** (sketch: a rectangular core with **two limbs**; the LV and HV windings are wound on the limbs, half of each winding on each limb, LV next to the core and HV outside it; the windings **surround the core**).
- Single magnetic circuit; flux path of one window around the core.
- Cylindrical (concentric) coils.

**Shell type** (sketch: a core with **three limbs**, the central limb twice as wide as the outer ones; both windings are on the central limb, interleaved as sandwich (disc) coils; the **core surrounds the windings**).
- Flux divides in the central limb and returns through the two outer limbs (double magnetic circuit).

| Feature | Core type | Shell type |
|---|---|---|
| Core surrounds windings? | No, windings surround core | Yes, core surrounds windings |
| Limbs | 2 | 3 (central limb carries winding) |
| Magnetic circuit | single | double (two parallel paths) |
| Windings | concentric cylindrical | sandwich / disc |
| Leakage reactance | higher | lower |
| Mechanical protection of winding | less | better (core shields winding) |
| Insulation, repair | easier to insulate and repair | difficult to inspect and repair |
| Cooling | better (more winding surface exposed) | poorer |
| Suitable for | high voltage, large ratings | low voltage, high current |

**Advantages and disadvantages**
- *Core type:* advantages: easy to assemble, insulate and repair; good natural cooling; suits high voltage. Disadvantages: larger leakage flux and reactance; less mechanical support to windings under short circuit.
- *Shell type:* advantages: lower leakage reactance; windings well supported and protected (withstand short-circuit forces); compact for low voltage high current. Disadvantages: difficult to dismantle and repair; poorer cooling; more iron.

**Equivalent circuit (exact, referred to primary)** (draw as described):
- Supply $V_1$, then series $R_1$ and $X_1$ (primary resistance and leakage reactance), carrying $I_1$.
- A shunt (magnetising) branch across $E_1$: $R_0$ (core loss, carries $I_w$) in parallel with $X_0$ (magnetising, carries $I_\mu$); together they draw $I_0$.
- Then series $R_2' = R_2/K^2$ and $X_2' = X_2/K^2$ carrying $I_2' = KI_2$, ending at the load terminals $V_2' = V_2/K$ with load $Z_L' = Z_L/K^2$.
- $\bar I_1 = \bar I_0 + \bar I_2'$.

**Approximate equivalent circuit:** the shunt branch $R_0 \parallel X_0$ is moved to the supply terminals (since $I_0$ is only 2-5% of $I_1$), so the series elements combine:
$$R_{01} = R_1 + \frac{R_2}{K^2}, \quad X_{01} = X_1 + \frac{X_2}{K^2}, \quad Z_{01} = \sqrt{R_{01}^2 + X_{01}^2}$$
with $K = N_2/N_1$. $R_0 = V_1/I_w$, $X_0 = V_1/I_\mu$.

**Phasor diagram on lagging pf load** (construction, take $\Phi$ as reference along the horizontal):
1. Draw $\Phi$ horizontally. $E_1$ and $E_2$ lag $\Phi$ by 90° (drawn vertically down).
2. $I_0$ leads $\Phi$ by the hysteretic angle; components $I_\mu$ (along $\Phi$) and $I_w$ (along $-E_1$).
3. Secondary: $I_2$ lags $V_2$ by $\phi_2$. Starting from $E_2$: $\bar V_2 = \bar E_2 - \bar I_2R_2 - j\bar I_2X_2$, i.e. subtract the drop $I_2R_2$ (parallel to $I_2$) and $I_2X_2$ (perpendicular to $I_2$) to reach $V_2$.
4. Primary: $I_2' = KI_2$ drawn antiphase to $I_2$; $\bar I_1 = \bar I_0 + \bar I_2'$ (parallelogram).
5. $-E_1$ drawn opposite $E_1$; $\bar V_1 = -\bar E_1 + \bar I_1R_1 + j\bar I_1X_1$ (add $I_1R_1$ parallel to $I_1$ and $I_1X_1$ leading $I_1$ by 90°).
6. $\phi_1$ is the angle between $V_1$ and $I_1$; it is slightly larger than $\phi_2$.

items.question_md:
A 10 kVA, 2500/250 V, 50Hz single phase transformer gave the following results

No load test- 250V, 0.8A, 50 W (LV side)

Short circuit test – 60V, 3A, 45 W (HV side)

Calculate:

(a) Component of no load current

(b) Calculate efficiency at $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{2}$, and 1 of full load at 0.8 pf lagging

(c) Calculate voltage regulation and secondary terminal voltage at full load 0.8 pf lagging
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 10 kVA, 2500/250 V. NL (LV): 250 V, 0.8 A, 50 W, so $P_i = 50$ W. SC (HV): 60 V, 3 A, 45 W. Rated HV current $= 10000/2500 = 4$ A.

**(a) Components of no-load current**
$$\cos\phi_0 = \frac{50}{250 \times 0.8} = 0.25, \quad \sin\phi_0 = 0.9682$$
$$I_w = 0.8 \times 0.25 = \mathbf{0.2\ A}, \qquad I_\mu = 0.8 \times 0.9682 = \mathbf{0.775\ A}$$

**(b) Efficiency at 0.8 pf**

SC test was at 3 A, not rated 4 A, so scale the copper loss:
$$P_{cu,fl} = 45\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 = 80\ \text{W}$$
$$\eta = \frac{x(10000)(0.8)}{x(10000)(0.8) + 50 + x^2(80)}$$

| Load $x$ | Output (W) | Cu loss (W) | Total loss (W) | $\eta$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1/4 | 2000 | 5 | 55 | **97.32%** |
| 1/2 | 4000 | 20 | 70 | **98.28%** |
| 1 | 8000 | 80 | 130 | **98.40%** |

**(c) Regulation and secondary voltage, full load 0.8 pf lagging**
$$Z_{01} = \frac{60}{3} = 20\ \Omega, \quad R_{01} = \frac{45}{3^2} = 5\ \Omega, \quad X_{01} = \sqrt{20^2 - 5^2} = 19.365\ \Omega$$
$$\%R = \frac{I_1(R_{01}\cos\phi + X_{01}\sin\phi)}{V_1}\times 100 = \frac{4(5 \times 0.8 + 19.365 \times 0.6)}{2500}\times 100 = \frac{62.48}{2500}\times 100$$
$$\boxed{\%R \approx 2.50\%}$$
$$V_2 = 250(1 - 0.02499) \approx \mathbf{243.75\ V}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Define the basic constructional features of a D.C. machine with the help of neat diagram. Also give the classification of DC Machines.
items.answer_md:
**Constructional features** (diagram: a cross-section showing the outer ring-shaped yoke, poles bolted inward with pole shoes and field coils, the slotted armature on the shaft at the centre, and the commutator with brushes at one end).

1. **Yoke:** outer cylindrical frame of cast iron/steel; mechanical support and return path for flux.
2. **Poles and pole shoes:** laminated steel; carry field coils, pole shoe spreads flux over the air gap.
3. **Field winding:** copper coils on poles; produce the main flux when excited.
4. **Armature core:** laminated silicon-steel slotted drum on the shaft; holds conductors, low-reluctance flux path.
5. **Armature winding:** copper conductors in slots (lap or wave); EMF induced / torque produced here.
6. **Commutator:** copper segments insulated by mica; converts AC in the armature into DC at the terminals.
7. **Brushes:** carbon; collect current from the commutator.
8. **Shaft and bearings:** carry the rotor and transmit mechanical power.

**Classification of DC machines** (by the way the field winding is excited)

1. **Separately excited:** field winding is fed from an independent DC source.
2. **Self-excited:** field is fed from the machine's own armature.
   - **Shunt:** field winding (many turns, thin wire, high resistance) in parallel with the armature.
   - **Series:** field winding (few turns, thick wire, low resistance) in series with the armature.
   - **Compound:** both shunt and series fields.
     - **Short shunt:** shunt field across the armature only.
     - **Long shunt:** shunt field across armature plus series field.
     - Also **cumulative** (series flux aids shunt flux) or **differential** (series flux opposes shunt flux).

Each type exists as both a **generator** and a **motor**. Permanent-magnet machines (field from magnets) are a special case of separate excitation.

items.question_md: A separately excited generator with constant excitation is connected to a constant resistance circuit. When the speed is 1200 r.p.m. it delivers 120 A at 500 V. At what speed will the current be reduced to 60 A? Armature resistance = $0.1\ \Omega$. Contact drop/brush = 1 V. Armature reaction may be ignored.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** separately excited, constant excitation so $\Phi$ constant; $N_1 = 1200$ rpm, $I_1 = 120$ A, $V_1 = 500$ V; $R_a = 0.1\ \Omega$; brush drop 1 V per brush, so $2$ V total; load resistance constant.

**To find:** speed $N_2$ at which $I_2 = 60$ A.

**Step 1: load resistance**
$$R_L = \frac{V_1}{I_1} = \frac{500}{120} = 4.167\ \Omega$$

**Step 2: generated EMF at 1200 rpm**
$$E_1 = V_1 + I_1R_a + 2V_b = 500 + 120(0.1) + 2 = 514\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: generated EMF for 60 A**
$$V_2 = I_2R_L = 60 \times 4.167 = 250\ \text{V}$$
$$E_2 = 250 + 60(0.1) + 2 = 258\ \text{V}$$

**Step 4: speed**

With constant flux $E \propto N$:
$$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{E_2}{E_1} \Rightarrow N_2 = 1200 \times \frac{258}{514}$$

**Result:** $N_2 \approx$ **602.3 rpm**

items.question_md: Explain input and output characteristics of Common Emitter transistor with diagram. Label the three operating regions. (Indicate there in the active, cut-off and saturation region).
items.answer_md:
### Circuit
NPN transistor with emitter common: $V_{BB}$ and a rheostat forward-bias the base-emitter junction, $V_{CC}$ and a rheostat supply the collector; microammeter in the base lead, milliammeter in the collector lead, voltmeters across BE and CE.

**Input characteristics** ($I_B$ vs $V_{BE}$ at constant $V_{CE}$). Circuit: base supply $V_{BB}$ through a rheostat, collector supply $V_{CC}$, ammeters for $I_B$ (μA) and $I_C$ (mA), voltmeters for $V_{BE}$ and $V_{CE}$.
- The curve is like a forward-biased diode: $I_B \approx 0$ until $V_{BE}$ reaches the cut-in voltage (about 0.5 to 0.7 V for Si), then rises steeply.
- Increasing $V_{CE}$ shifts the curve slightly to the **right** (less $I_B$ for the same $V_{BE}$), because the wider collector depletion region narrows the base (Early effect) and less recombination occurs in the base.
- Input resistance $r_i = \dfrac{\Delta V_{BE}}{\Delta I_B}\Big|_{V_{CE}}$, typically about 1 kΩ (low).

**Output characteristics** ($I_C$ vs $V_{CE}$ at constant $I_B$, a family of curves for $I_B = 0, 20, 40, 60\ \mu A, \dots$):
- For each $I_B$, $I_C$ rises steeply for very small $V_{CE}$ (0 to about 0.2 to 0.3 V) and then becomes almost flat, rising only slightly with $V_{CE}$ (Early effect).
- In the flat portion $I_C \approx \beta I_B$; higher $I_B$ gives a higher curve.
- Output resistance $r_o = \dfrac{\Delta V_{CE}}{\Delta I_C}\Big|_{I_B}$ (high, tens of kΩ); current gain $\beta = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}\Big|_{V_{CE}}$ (50 to 300).

**Regions (mark them on the output graph):**
| Region | Where on the graph | Junction bias | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active | flat part of the curves, above $I_B = 0$ and right of the knee | BE forward, CB reverse | amplifier |
| Saturation | steep rising part near the vertical axis, $V_{CE} \le V_{CE(sat)} \approx 0.2$ V | both junctions forward | switch ON |
| Cut-off | below the $I_B = 0$ curve, $I_C = I_{CEO}$ (small, not exactly 0) | both junctions reverse (or BE not forward) | switch OFF |

**Load line:** for a collector resistor $R_C$, $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_CR_C$ is a straight line from $(V_{CC}, 0)$ to $(0, V_{CC}/R_C)$; its intersection with the curve of the chosen $I_B$ is the operating point (Q-point), placed in the middle of the active region for amplification.

items.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers
items.question_md:
A diode crystal having internal resistance $r_f = 25\ \Omega$ is used for half-wave rectification. If the applied voltage $v = 60 \sin \omega t$ and load resistance = $725\ \Omega$, find:

(i) $I_{max}$, $I_{dc}$, $I_{rms}$. (ii) A.C. input power and D.C. output power.

(iii) D.C. output voltage. (iv) Efficiency of rectification.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $r_f = 25\ \Omega$, $R_L = 725\ \Omega$, $v = 60\sin\omega t$ so $V_m = 60$ V, half-wave.

**(i) Currents**
$$I_{max} = \frac{V_m}{r_f + R_L} = \frac{60}{750} = \mathbf{0.08\ A = 80\ mA}$$
$$I_{dc} = \frac{I_{max}}{\pi} = \frac{0.08}{\pi} = \mathbf{25.46\ mA}$$
$$I_{rms} = \frac{I_{max}}{2} = \mathbf{40\ mA}$$

**(ii) Powers**
$$P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(r_f + R_L) = (0.04)^2 \times 750 = \mathbf{1.2\ W}$$
$$P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = (0.02546)^2 \times 725 = \mathbf{0.470\ W}$$

**(iii) DC output voltage**
$$V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = 0.02546 \times 725 = \mathbf{18.46\ V}$$

**(iv) Efficiency of rectification**
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{0.470}{1.2} = \mathbf{39.2\%}$$
Check: $\eta = \dfrac{0.406}{1 + r_f/R_L} = \dfrac{0.406}{1 + 25/725} = 39.2\%$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the condition of maximum power transfer in any D.C. circuit and find the efficiency when the source is transferring maximum power to the load.
items.answer_md:
### Statement
A linear DC network delivers maximum power to a load resistance $R_L$ when $R_L$ equals the Thevenin (internal) resistance of the network seen from the load terminals: $R_L = R_{th}$.

### Derivation
1. Replace the network by its Thevenin equivalent: $V_{th}$ in series with $R_{th}$, connected to $R_L$.
2. Load current:
$$I = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + R_L}$$
3. Power in the load:
$$P_L = I^2R_L = \frac{V_{th}^2\,R_L}{(R_{th} + R_L)^2}$$
4. $V_{th}$ and $R_{th}$ are fixed; vary $R_L$. For maximum, $\dfrac{dP_L}{dR_L} = 0$:
$$\frac{dP_L}{dR_L} = V_{th}^2\,\frac{(R_{th} + R_L)^2 - R_L \cdot 2(R_{th} + R_L)}{(R_{th} + R_L)^4} = 0$$
5. Hence $(R_{th} + R_L) - 2R_L = 0$, giving
$$\boxed{R_L = R_{th}}$$
(The second derivative is negative here, so this is a maximum.)
6. Maximum power:
$$P_{max} = \frac{V_{th}^2 R_{th}}{(2R_{th})^2} = \boxed{\frac{V_{th}^2}{4R_{th}}}$$

### Efficiency at maximum power transfer
Power produced by the source: $P_{in} = V_{th}I = \dfrac{V_{th}^2}{2R_{th}}$. Half of it is lost in $R_{th}$.
$$\eta = \frac{P_{max}}{P_{in}} = \frac{V_{th}^2/4R_{th}}{V_{th}^2/2R_{th}} = \frac{R_L}{R_L + R_{th}} = \mathbf{50\%}$$

**Remark:** maximum power transfer is not maximum efficiency. It is used in communication and electronic circuits, where the signal power is small; power systems are run with $R_L \gg R_{th}$ for high efficiency.

items.question_md:
Determine the current $I_1$ in the circuit of given figure using Superposition theorem.

[Figure: A 12 V DC source (+ at top) on the left. Its top terminal connects through a 2 Ω resistor, carrying current $I_1$ flowing to the right, to a top node. From the top node two branches go to the bottom rail: a 3 Ω resistor in series with a 6 A current source pointing downward, and a 6 Ω resistor in series with an 8 V DC source (+ at top). The bottom rail returns to the negative terminal of the 12 V source.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 12 V (+ top) with 2 Ω carrying $I_1$ to top node T; branch 3 Ω + 6 A (down) from T; branch 6 Ω + 8 V (+ top) from T.

**(i) 12 V alone** (6 A opened, 8 V shorted): the 3 Ω branch is open, so 12 V drives 2 Ω + 6 Ω:
$$I_1' = \frac{12}{2 + 6} = 1.5\ \text{A}$$

**(ii) 6 A alone** (both voltage sources shorted): 6 A is drawn out of T, supplied by the 2 Ω and 6 Ω paths in parallel. Current divider:
$$I_1'' = 6 \times \frac{6}{2 + 6} = 4.5\ \text{A}\ (\text{towards T, same sense as } I_1)$$

**(iii) 8 V alone** (12 V shorted, 6 A opened): 8 V drives 6 Ω + 2 Ω; current flows from T back through 2 Ω to the left, opposite to $I_1$:
$$I_1^{\prime\prime\prime} = -\frac{8}{6 + 2} = -1\ \text{A}$$

**Total:**
$$I_1 = 1.5 + 4.5 - 1 = \mathbf{5\ A}$$

Check: $V_T = 12 - 2(5) = 2$ V; 6 Ω branch: $(2 - 8)/6 = -1$ A; KCL at T: $5 = 6 + (-1)$. ✓

In the given circuit, find the values of:

(i) the current I (ii) V1 and V2 and (iii) Power factor. Draw the phasor diagram.

items.answer_md:

- $V_2 = IZ_2 = 5.838\times37.94 = $ **221.5 V**, at $-29.33^\circ$ to $V$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Describe the phenomenon of resonance in parallel circuit and explain its Q factor. Why parallel resonance circuit is often regarded as rejector circuit?
items.answer_md:
**Parallel resonance**

Consider a practical coil ($R$, $L$) in parallel with a capacitor $C$, fed by a variable-frequency source $V$.

- Coil current $I_L = V/Z_L$, lagging $V$ by $\phi_L$, where $Z_L = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$, $\cos\phi_L = R/Z_L$, $\sin\phi_L = X_L/Z_L$.
- Capacitor current $I_C = V/X_C$, leading $V$ by $90^\circ$.

**Condition:** resonance occurs when the supply current is in phase with $V$, i.e. the reactive (quadrature) components cancel:
$$I_L\sin\phi_L = I_C \Rightarrow \frac{V}{Z_L}\cdot\frac{X_L}{Z_L} = \frac{V}{X_C} \Rightarrow Z_L^2 = X_LX_C = \frac{L}{C}$$
$$R^2 + (2\pi f_0L)^2 = \frac{L}{C} \Rightarrow \boxed{f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC} - \frac{R^2}{L^2}}}$$
(reduces to $1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$ when $R$ is negligible).

**Current and impedance at resonance:** only the active component $I_L\cos\phi_L$ flows from the supply:
$$I_0 = \frac{V}{Z_L}\cdot\frac{R}{Z_L} = \frac{VR}{L/C} = \frac{V}{L/(CR)}$$
so the circuit behaves as a pure resistance, the **dynamic impedance** $Z_D = \dfrac{L}{CR}$, which is **maximum**; the line current is **minimum** and the power factor is unity.

**Q factor:** at parallel resonance the current circulating between L and C is many times the line current; Q is the **current magnification**:
$$Q = \frac{I_C}{I_0} = \frac{\omega_0L}{R}\ \left(\approx \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\right)$$
A higher Q gives a sharper response (smaller bandwidth $f_0/Q$).

**Why it is called a rejector circuit:** at the resonant frequency its impedance $L/CR$ is maximum and the line current minimum, so the circuit **rejects** (strongly opposes) currents of that frequency while passing others. It is used in radio receivers and filters (wave traps) to reject an unwanted frequency. By contrast the series resonant circuit, with minimum impedance, is an *acceptor* circuit.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
In a 50 kVA, 1100/220 V transformer, the iron and copper losses at full load are 350 W and 425 W, respectively. Calculate the efficiency at
\ni. half load with unity power factor

ii. full load with 0.8 power factor lagging and

iii. Maximum Efficiency and the load at which maximum efficiency occurs assuming the load to be resistive.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 50 kVA, 1100/220 V; $P_i = 350$ W, $P_{cu,fl} = 425$ W.

**(i) Half load, unity pf**
$$\text{Output} = 0.5 \times 50000 \times 1 = 25000\ \text{W}, \quad P_{cu} = 0.5^2 \times 425 = 106.25\ \text{W}$$
$$\eta = \frac{25000}{25000 + 350 + 106.25}\times 100 = \mathbf{98.21\%}$$

**(ii) Full load, 0.8 pf lagging**
$$\text{Output} = 50000 \times 0.8 = 40000\ \text{W}$$
$$\eta = \frac{40000}{40000 + 350 + 425}\times 100 = \frac{40000}{40775}\times 100 = \mathbf{98.10\%}$$

**(iii) Maximum efficiency (resistive load, unity pf)**

Load at maximum efficiency (copper loss = iron loss):
$$x = \sqrt{\frac{350}{425}} = 0.9075 \Rightarrow \text{load} = 0.9075 \times 50 = \mathbf{45.37\ kVA}$$
Output $= 45374$ W, losses $= 2 \times 350 = 700$ W:
$$\eta_{max} = \frac{45374}{45374 + 700}\times 100 = \mathbf{98.48\%}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Transformer phasor diagrams and equivalent circuit
items.question_md: Draw the equivalent circuit diagram of the transformer referred to secondary side. Draw the phasor diagram for this circuit and determine voltage regulation expression for lagging p.f. load.
items.answer_md:
**Equivalent circuit referred to secondary** ($K = N_2/N_1$)

Primary quantities are transferred to the secondary side:
$$V_1' = KV_1, \quad R_1' = K^2R_1, \quad X_1' = K^2X_1, \quad R_0' = K^2R_0, \quad X_0' = K^2X_0$$
Combining with the secondary's own $R_2$, $X_2$ (approximate circuit, shunt branch moved to the input):
$$R_{02} = R_2 + K^2R_1, \qquad X_{02} = X_2 + K^2X_1, \qquad Z_{02} = \sqrt{R_{02}^2 + X_{02}^2}$$
Circuit: input terminals at $KV_1$ (= $E_2$ on no load), shunt branch $R_0' \parallel X_0'$, then series $R_{02}$ and $X_{02}$ carrying $I_2$ to the load $Z_L$ at terminal voltage $V_2$.

**Phasor diagram (lagging pf $\cos\phi$)**

Take $I_2$ along the horizontal reference.
1. $V_2$ leads $I_2$ by $\phi$: $OA = V_2$.
2. From $A$, draw $AB = I_2R_{02}$ parallel to $I_2$.
3. From $B$, draw $BC = I_2X_{02}$ perpendicular to $I_2$ (leading).
4. $OC = E_2 = KV_1$ (no-load secondary voltage): $\bar E_2 = \bar V_2 + \bar I_2(R_{02} + jX_{02})$.

**Regulation expression**

Drop a perpendicular from $C$ onto the extension of $OA$ (meeting it at $D$). Since the angle between $OC$ and $OA$ is small, $OC \approx OD$:
$$E_2 \approx V_2 + I_2R_{02}\cos\phi + I_2X_{02}\sin\phi$$
So the drop is
$$E_2 - V_2 \approx I_2R_{02}\cos\phi + I_2X_{02}\sin\phi$$
$$\boxed{\%\,\text{regulation} = \frac{E_2 - V_2}{E_2}\times 100 = \frac{I_2(R_{02}\cos\phi + X_{02}\sin\phi)}{E_2}\times 100}$$
(For leading pf the sign of the $X_{02}\sin\phi$ term becomes negative.) In per-unit form: $\%R = \epsilon_r\cos\phi + \epsilon_x\sin\phi$, with $\epsilon_r = I_2R_{02}/E_2$ and $\epsilon_x = I_2X_{02}/E_2$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: What are the main parts of D C Machine? Write the function of each part and state the material of which each part is made?
items.answer_md:
| Part | Function | Material |
|---|---|---|
| **Yoke** (frame) | Mechanical support and protective cover; carries the magnetic flux between poles | Cast iron (small machines), cast steel or rolled steel (large machines) |
| **Pole core and pole shoe** | Carry the field winding; pole shoe spreads flux uniformly over the air gap and supports the coils | Laminated cast steel / sheet steel |
| **Field winding** | Carries current to produce the main magnetic flux | Enamelled copper wire |
| **Armature core** | Houses armature conductors in slots; gives low-reluctance path for flux | Laminated silicon steel (0.35-0.5 mm sheets) to reduce eddy and hysteresis loss |
| **Armature winding** | EMF is induced in it (generator) / it carries current to produce torque (motor) | Copper conductors, lap or wave connected |
| **Commutator** | Converts alternating EMF/current in the armature into unidirectional at the terminals (mechanical rectifier); connects armature to the external circuit | Hard-drawn copper segments insulated by mica |
| **Brushes** | Collect current from (or feed current to) the rotating commutator | Carbon or graphite (self-lubricating, soft) |
| **Shaft and bearings** | Transmit mechanical power; support the rotor with low friction | Mild steel shaft; ball or roller bearings |
| **Interpoles** (if fitted) | Improve commutation | Steel core with copper winding |

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Develop an expression for the speed of a dc motor in terms of back emf and flux per pole.
items.answer_md:
**Step 1: back EMF.** When the armature of a motor rotates, its conductors cut flux and an EMF is induced which opposes the supply (Lenz's law). Its magnitude is given by the EMF equation:
$$E_b = \frac{P\Phi ZN}{60A}$$
where $P$ = poles, $\Phi$ = flux per pole (Wb), $Z$ = armature conductors, $N$ = speed (rpm), $A$ = parallel paths.

**Step 2: voltage equation of the motor.** Applied voltage = back EMF + armature drop:
$$V = E_b + I_aR_a \Rightarrow E_b = V - I_aR_a$$

**Step 3: equate.**
$$\frac{P\Phi ZN}{60A} = V - I_aR_a$$
$$N = \frac{60A}{PZ}\cdot\frac{V - I_aR_a}{\Phi} = \frac{60A}{PZ}\cdot\frac{E_b}{\Phi}$$

For a given machine $\dfrac{60A}{PZ} = k$ is constant, so
$$\boxed{N = k\,\frac{E_b}{\Phi} \quad\text{i.e.}\quad N \propto \frac{E_b}{\Phi}}$$

**Step 4: comparing two operating points** of the same machine:
$$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{E_{b2}}{E_{b1}}\times\frac{\Phi_1}{\Phi_2}$$

**Conclusions**
- Speed is directly proportional to back EMF and inversely proportional to flux per pole.
- Weakening the field raises the speed; this is why a shunt motor must never run with its field open, and a series motor must never be started on no load (flux very small, speed dangerously high).
- For a shunt motor ($\Phi$ constant), $N_2/N_1 = E_{b2}/E_{b1}$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Draw and explain V-I characteristic of P-N Junction diode when it is (i) forward biased (ii) reverse biased.
items.answer_md:
**(i) Forward bias**

**Forward bias** (P to + terminal, N to − terminal):
- The applied voltage opposes the barrier, so the depletion layer **narrows** and the barrier falls.
- Below the **cut-in (knee) voltage** $V_\gamma$ (0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge) the current is very small.
- Above $V_\gamma$, majority carriers cross freely and the current rises **exponentially** (in mA), limited only by the external resistance and the small bulk resistance $r_f$.

**(ii) Reverse bias**

**Reverse bias** (P to − terminal, N to + terminal):
- The applied voltage aids the barrier, so the depletion layer **widens** and majority carriers cannot cross.
- Only a tiny **reverse saturation current** $I_0$ flows, due to **minority carriers** (nA for Si, μA for Ge). It is almost independent of voltage but roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise.
- At the **breakdown voltage** $V_{BR}$ the reverse current rises sharply.

**V-I characteristic** (draw it with labels):
- First quadrant (forward): current ≈ 0 up to $V_\gamma$, then a steep exponential rise; current axis in **mA**.
- Third quadrant (reverse): a small, nearly flat current $-I_0$ (axis in **μA**, a different scale, which must be marked), then a sharp vertical drop at $-V_{BR}$.
- Mark $V_\gamma$, $I_0$ and $V_{BR}$.

The curve follows the diode equation
$$I = I_0\left(e^{V/\eta V_T} - 1\right), \qquad V_T = \frac{kT}{q} \approx 26\ \text{mV at 300 K}$$
with $\eta = 1$ for Ge and $\eta = 2$ for Si (Rajput).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers
items.question_md: Drive the expression of output voltage and efficiency of full wave rectifier.
items.answer_md:
**Circuit assumed:** full-wave (centre-tap or bridge); in each half cycle one conducting path of forward resistance $r_f$ feeds the load $R_L$. Each half of the secondary gives $v = V_m\sin\theta$, $\theta = \omega t$.

**Derivation** (diode resistance $r_f$, load $R_L$, $\theta = \omega t$). In each half cycle one path conducts, so the load current is
$$i = I_m\sin\theta \ \ (0 \le \theta \le \pi), \qquad I_m = \frac{V_m}{r_f + R_L}$$
and the same hump repeats every $\pi$.

*DC (average) current:*
$$I_{dc} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{I_m}{\pi}\big[-\cos\theta\big]_0^{\pi} = \frac{2I_m}{\pi}$$
so $V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = \dfrac{2I_mR_L}{\pi} \approx \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}$ when $r_f \ll R_L$.

*RMS current:*
$$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta} = \sqrt{\frac{I_m^2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}} = \frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$$

*Efficiency:*
$$P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = \frac{4I_m^2}{\pi^2}R_L, \qquad P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(r_f + R_L) = \frac{I_m^2}{2}(r_f + R_L)$$
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{R_L}{r_f + R_L} = \frac{0.812}{1 + r_f/R_L}$$
**Maximum efficiency** (when $r_f \ll R_L$): $\mathbf{\eta_{max} = 81.2\%}$, twice the half-wave value of 40.6%.

**Output voltage summary:** $V_{dc} = \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi} = 0.637V_m$ (ideal diodes), $V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt2}$, ripple frequency $2f$.

items.question_md:
Find the current $I$ supplied by the d.c. source in the circuit shown in Fig.

[Figure: A 30 V d.c. source drives current $I$ into a resistor network. At the top is a triangle of two 2 Ω resistors meeting at an apex. A 4 Ω resistor runs horizontally across the base of that triangle. Below it, on the left and on the right, are pairs of 2 Ω resistors forming two inverted-V branches. Two 1 Ω resistors run along the bottom and return to the source.]
items.answer_md:
The figure description does not say which nodes the inverted-V branches and the two 1 Ω resistors join, or where the source connects, so the numerical value of $I$ cannot be fixed from the description. The method is:

**Step 1: Delta-star on the top triangle.** The apex X and the base nodes L and R form a delta: X-L 2 Ω, X-R 2 Ω, L-R 4 Ω ($\Sigma = 8\ \Omega$). Star equivalent, centre S:
$$R_{SX} = \frac{2 \times 2}{8} = 0.5\ \Omega,\quad R_{SL} = \frac{2 \times 4}{8} = 1\ \Omega,\quad R_{SR} = \frac{2 \times 4}{8} = 1\ \Omega$$

**Step 2: Redraw** with the source connected to X (through 0.5 Ω to S), and S feeding the two lower inverted-V branches through 1 Ω each.

**Step 3: Reduce** the lower part: each inverted-V of two 2 Ω arms, together with the 1 Ω bottom resistors, is combined by series-parallel (or a second delta-star if it forms a bridge) to a single $R_{eq}$ seen by the source.

**Step 4:**
$$I = \frac{30}{R_{eq}}$$

**Figure detail needed:** the end nodes of the four lower 2 Ω resistors and of the two 1 Ω resistors, and the node to which the source's negative terminal returns.

items.question_md:
Find Norton's equivalent across the terminal A-B.

[Figure: The left branch is a 10 A current source (arrow upward) in series with a 20 V voltage source (+ on top). The right branch is a 6 Ω resistor in series with a 3 Ω resistor. The top node is terminal A. A middle wire joins the junction between the two sources to the junction between the 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors. The bottom of the 3 Ω resistor and the bottom of the 20 V source connect to terminal B.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading:** left branch from B upward: 20 V source (+ top) to junction J, then the 10 A source (arrow up) from J to A. Right branch: 6 Ω from A to J′ and 3 Ω from J′ to B. The middle wire joins J and J′.

**Step 1: $I_N$ (short A-B, so $V_A = 0$).** $V_J = 20$ V. Current into A from the 10 A source is 10 A; current from J to A through 6 Ω is $\dfrac{20 - 0}{6} = 3.333$ A.
$$I_N = 10 + 3.333 = \mathbf{13.33\ A}\ (\text{A to B through the short})$$
(The 3 Ω sits directly across the 20 V source and does not affect the result.)

**Step 2: $R_N$** (10 A opened, 20 V shorted, so J is joined to B and the 3 Ω is shorted out):
$$R_N = \mathbf{6\ \Omega}$$

**Norton equivalent:** 13.33 A in parallel with 6 Ω (current directed towards A).

Check: open-circuit voltage $V_{AB} = 20 + 6 \times 10 = 80$ V and $I_N R_N = 13.33 \times 6 = 80$ V.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the expression for impedance, power factor, phase angle and power for an R-L-C series circuit. Draw phasor diagram also. Derive the expression of resonant frequency.
items.answer_md:
### Circuit
$R$, $L$, $C$ in series across $v = V_m\sin\omega t$; the same current $I$ (rms) flows through all three, so take $I$ as the **reference phasor** (horizontal).

### Phasor diagram (described)
- $V_R = IR$ in phase with $I$ (along $I$).
- $V_L = IX_L$ leading $I$ by 90° (vertically up), $X_L = \omega L$.
- $V_C = IX_C$ lagging $I$ by 90° (vertically down), $X_C = 1/\omega C$.
- For $X_L > X_C$: net vertical phasor $V_L - V_C$ upward; the resultant $V$ is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides $V_R$ and $(V_L - V_C)$, leading $I$ by $\phi$.

### 1. Impedance
$$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$
$$\boxed{Z = \frac{V}{I} = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}},\qquad \bar Z = R + j(X_L - X_C)$$

### 2. Phase angle
From the voltage triangle:
$$\boxed{\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L - X_C}{R}}$$
$X_L > X_C$: current lags (inductive); $X_L < X_C$: current leads (capacitive); $X_L = X_C$: $\phi = 0$.

### 3. Power factor
$$\boxed{\cos\phi = \frac{V_R}{V} = \frac{R}{Z}}$$

### 4. Power
With $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$:
$$p = vi = V_mI_m\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$
The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so
$$\boxed{P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\phi = VI\cos\phi = I^2R\ \text{watts}}$$
Only $R$ consumes power; $L$ and $C$ exchange energy with the source.

### 5. Resonant frequency
Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$:
$$\omega_0L = \frac{1}{\omega_0C}\Rightarrow \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad \boxed{f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\ \text{Hz}}$$
At $f_0$: $Z = R$ (minimum), $I = V/R$ (maximum), $\cos\phi = 1$, and $V_L = V_C$ cancel each other.

items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance 12 μF. Estimate:

(i) the frequency at which resonance will occur.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** coil $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$; $C = 12\ \mu$F $= 12\times10^{-6}$ F.

$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{0.64 \times 12\times10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{7.68\times10^{-6}}}$$
$$\boxed{f_0 = 57.43\ \text{Hz}}\quad(\omega_0 = 360.84\ \text{rad/s})$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance 12 μF. Estimate:

(ii) the voltage across the coil and capacitor, respectively and also the supply voltage when a current of 1.5 A at the resonant frequency is flowing.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$, $C = 12\ \mu$F, $I = 1.5$ A at $f_0 = 57.43$ Hz ($\omega_0 = 360.84$ rad/s).

**Reactances at resonance:**
$$X_L = \omega_0L = 360.84 \times 0.64 = 230.94\ \Omega,\qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega_0C} = 230.94\ \Omega$$

**Voltage across the coil** (coil has $R$ and $L$):
$$Z_{coil} = \sqrt{40^2 + 230.94^2} = 234.38\ \Omega$$
$$V_{coil} = IZ_{coil} = 1.5 \times 234.38 = \boxed{351.6\ \text{V}}$$

**Voltage across the capacitor:**
$$V_C = IX_C = 1.5 \times 230.94 = \boxed{346.4\ \text{V}}$$

**Supply voltage:** at resonance $Z = R$
$$V = IR = 1.5 \times 40 = \boxed{60\ \text{V}}$$

The coil and capacitor voltages are each nearly 6 times the supply voltage ($Q = 230.94/40 = 5.77$), because their reactive parts cancel.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance 12 μF. Estimate:

(iii) the three voltages in (ii) (the voltage across the coil, the voltage across the capacitor and the supply voltage) with a current of 1.5 A flowing at a frequency of 50 Hz.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** coil $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$; $C = 12\ \mu F$; $I = 1.5$ A, $f = 50$ Hz.

**Reactances**
- $X_L = 2\pi(50)(0.64) = 201.06\ \Omega$
- $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(50)(12\times10^{-6})} = 265.26\ \Omega$

**1. Voltage across the coil**
$$Z_{coil} = \sqrt{40^2 + 201.06^2} = 205.00\ \Omega,\qquad V_{coil} = 1.5\times205.00 = \mathbf{307.5\ V}$$
(leading $I$ by $\tan^{-1}(201.06/40) = 78.75^\circ$)

**2. Voltage across the capacitor**
$$V_C = IX_C = 1.5\times265.26 = \mathbf{397.9\ V}\ (\text{lagging } I \text{ by } 90^\circ)$$

**3. Supply voltage**
$$Z = \sqrt{40^2 + (201.06 - 265.26)^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 64.20^2} = 75.64\ \Omega$$
$$V = IZ = 1.5\times75.64 = \mathbf{113.5\ V}$$
The circuit is net capacitive, so the current leads the supply voltage by $\tan^{-1}(64.20/40) = 58.07^\circ$.

Note: $V_{coil}$ and $V_C$ are each larger than the supply voltage because they are nearly in antiphase and add as phasors.

items.topic: Transformer phasor diagrams and equivalent circuit
items.question_md: Draw and explain the phasor diagram of transformer when it is operating under no-load. Modify the above phasor diagram to take into account the loading effect (lagging) on the transformer.
items.answer_md:
**Operation on no load** (secondary open, $I_2 = 0$)

- With rated $V_1$ applied, the primary draws a small no-load current $I_0$ (2-5% of rated current).
- $I_0$ sets up the alternating mutual flux $\Phi$ which induces $E_1$ (opposing $V_1$, so $V_1 \approx -E_1$) and $E_2$; $V_2 = E_2$.
- A practical transformer has core loss and small primary copper loss, so $I_0$ is not purely magnetising. It has two components:
  - **Magnetising component** $I_\mu = I_0\sin\phi_0$: in phase with $\Phi$, produces the flux, wattless.
  - **Working (active) component** $I_w = I_0\cos\phi_0$: in phase with $V_1$, supplies the iron loss.
$$I_0 = \sqrt{I_w^2 + I_\mu^2}, \qquad \tan\phi_0 = \frac{I_\mu}{I_w}, \qquad P_i = V_1I_0\cos\phi_0$$
- Since $I_\mu \gg I_w$, $\cos\phi_0$ is low (0.1-0.3) and $\phi_0$ is close to 90°.

**No-load phasor diagram** (construction):
1. Draw flux $\Phi$ as the horizontal reference.
2. $E_1$ and $E_2$ lag $\Phi$ by 90° (drawn vertically downward); their lengths are in ratio $N_1 : N_2$.
3. $V_1$ is equal and opposite to $E_1$ (vertically upward).
4. $I_\mu$ along $\Phi$; $I_w$ along $V_1$; their resultant $I_0$ lags $V_1$ by $\phi_0$ (close to 90°), and leads $\Phi$ by the small hysteretic angle $\alpha = 90^\circ - \phi_0$.

**On load (lagging pf)**

- A load draws $I_2$ lagging $V_2$ by $\phi_2$. Its MMF $N_2I_2$ opposes the flux; the primary immediately draws an extra load component $I_2' = KI_2$ ($K = N_2/N_1$) antiphase to $I_2$, whose MMF cancels $N_2I_2$. So the flux stays nearly constant, and
$$\bar I_1 = \bar I_0 + \bar I_2'$$
- Winding resistances and leakage reactances cause drops:
$$\bar V_2 = \bar E_2 - \bar I_2(R_2 + jX_2), \qquad \bar V_1 = -\bar E_1 + \bar I_1(R_1 + jX_1)$$

**Phasor diagram on lagging load** (construction):
1. Start from the no-load diagram: $\Phi$ horizontal, $E_1$, $E_2$ 90° behind it, $I_0$ near $-E_1$ direction leading $\Phi$ by the hysteretic angle.
2. **Secondary side:** draw $I_2$ lagging the (yet to be found) $V_2$ by $\phi_2$. From $E_2$ subtract $I_2R_2$ (parallel to $I_2$) and $I_2X_2$ (perpendicular, leading $I_2$) to get $V_2$; $V_2 < E_2$.
3. **Primary current:** draw $I_2' = KI_2$ in direct opposition to $I_2$; add $I_0$ by parallelogram to get $I_1$.
4. **Primary voltage:** draw $-E_1$ opposite $E_1$; add $I_1R_1$ parallel to $I_1$ and $I_1X_1$ 90° ahead of $I_1$; the closing phasor is $V_1$.
5. $\phi_1$, the angle between $V_1$ and $I_1$, is slightly greater than $\phi_2$ (because of $I_0$), so the input pf is slightly lower than the load pf.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain armature resistance and field flux speed control method for DC motor.
items.answer_md:
**Basis:** for a DC motor $E_b = V - I_aR_a = \dfrac{P\Phi ZN}{60A}$, so
$$N \propto \frac{V - I_aR_a}{\Phi}$$

**1. Armature resistance (rheostatic) control**
- A variable resistance $R$ is put in series with the armature (shunt field connected directly across the supply, so $\Phi$ stays constant; for a series motor the resistance is in series with the whole motor).
- $N \propto V - I_a(R_a + R)$. Increasing $R$ increases the voltage drop, reduces $E_b$ and lowers the speed.
- Gives speeds **below** rated speed only.
- Drawbacks: large $I_a^2R$ loss in the resistance (poor efficiency), and speed changes considerably with load (poor regulation).
- Used where low speed is needed for short periods (cranes, hoists).

**2. Field flux control**
- Shunt motor: a rheostat in series with the shunt field. Series motor: a diverter resistance across the series field (or tapped field).
- Increasing field resistance reduces $I_{sh}$ and $\Phi$; since $N \propto 1/\Phi$, speed **rises**.
- Gives speeds **above** rated speed only.
- Advantages: field current is small, so rheostat loss is small (efficient), easy and smooth control.
- Limitation: a very weak field causes poor commutation and instability, which sets the upper speed limit.

| | Armature resistance control | Field flux control |
|---|---|---|
| Speed range | below rated | above rated |
| Loss | high ($I_a^2R$) | low ($I_{sh}^2R$) |
| Efficiency | poor | good |
| Speed regulation | poor | good |

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain Construction and working principle of a 1-Φ Transformer. Also give the classification of Transformers.
items.answer_md:
**Construction**
1. **Core:** laminated CRGO silicon steel (0.35-0.5 mm sheets, insulated by varnish). Silicon steel reduces hysteresis loss, lamination reduces eddy-current loss. Gives a low-reluctance path for the mutual flux.
2. **Windings:** primary ($N_1$ turns, connected to supply) and secondary ($N_2$ turns, connected to load), of insulated copper; LV winding placed next to the core, HV outside it.
3. **Insulation:** paper, pressboard, varnish between turns, layers and windings.
4. **Tank and transformer oil** (large units): oil insulates and cools; **conservator** takes up oil expansion; **breather** (silica gel) dries the incoming air; bushings bring out the leads; Buchholz relay protects against internal faults.
5. **Core type** (windings surround the core) or **shell type** (core surrounds the windings).

**Working principle (mutual induction)**
- An AC voltage $V_1$ applied to the primary draws a small magnetising current, setting up an alternating flux $\Phi = \Phi_m\sin\omega t$ in the core.
- This flux links both windings and, by Faraday's law, induces EMFs $E_1 = 4.44fN_1\Phi_m$ in the primary (opposing $V_1$, so $E_1 \approx V_1$) and $E_2 = 4.44fN_2\Phi_m$ in the secondary.
- Hence $\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} \approx \dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = K$. When a load is connected, the secondary current $I_2$ flows and the primary draws an extra $I_2' = KI_2$ to balance its MMF, so power is transferred at the same frequency: ideally $V_1I_1 = V_2I_2$.
- A transformer does not work on DC since $d\Phi/dt = 0$.

**Classification**
1. **Construction:** core type, shell type, berry type.
2. **Voltage:** step-up, step-down, isolation (1:1).
3. **Phases:** single-phase, three-phase.
4. **Application:** power, distribution, instrument (CT, PT), auto-transformer.
5. **Cooling:** dry (air) type, oil-immersed (ONAN, ONAF, OFAF), water-cooled.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: A 100 kVA transformer has an iron loss of 1 kW and a copper loss of 1.5 kW on normal output current. Calculate the kVA loading at which the efficiency is maximum, and the efficiency at this loading (a) at unity power factor, (b) at 0.8 power factor.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 100 kVA, $P_i = 1$ kW, $P_{cu,fl} = 1.5$ kW.

**kVA loading for maximum efficiency** (copper loss = iron loss):
$$x = \sqrt{\frac{P_i}{P_{cu,fl}}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{1.5}} = 0.8165$$
$$\text{kVA} = 0.8165 \times 100 = \mathbf{81.65\ kVA}$$

At this load, copper loss $= 1$ kW, total loss $= 2$ kW.

**(a) Unity pf**
$$\eta_{max} = \frac{81.65}{81.65 + 2}\times 100 = \mathbf{97.61\%}$$

**(b) 0.8 pf**
$$\text{Output} = 81.65 \times 0.8 = 65.32\ \text{kW}, \quad \eta_{max} = \frac{65.32}{65.32 + 2}\times 100 = \mathbf{97.03\%}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers
items.answer_md:
## Part 1: Full-wave centre-tap rectifier

**Circuit (centre-tap):** a transformer with a centre-tapped secondary; diode $D_1$ from the top end A and diode $D_2$ from the bottom end B, their cathodes joined at one end of $R_L$; the other end of $R_L$ goes to the centre tap C. Each half of the secondary supplies $V_m\sin\omega t$.

**Working:**
1. **Positive half cycle** (A positive w.r.t. C): $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts; $D_2$ is reverse biased. Current flows A, $D_1$, $R_L$ (top to bottom), C.
2. **Negative half cycle** (B positive w.r.t. C): $D_2$ conducts, $D_1$ is off. Current flows B, $D_2$, $R_L$ (same direction, top to bottom), C.
3. So the load current flows in the **same direction in both half cycles**: the output is a series of positive half-sine humps.
4. The non-conducting diode sees the whole secondary voltage, so **PIV $= 2V_m$** for the centre-tap circuit ($V_m$ for a bridge).

**Waveforms** (drawn one under the other on the same time axis):
- Input: sine wave $V_m\sin\omega t$ with period $T$.
- $i_{D1}$: humps in $0$ to $T/2$ only; $i_{D2}$: humps in $T/2$ to $T$ only.
- Load voltage $v_L$: a hump in every half cycle, peak $V_m$ (less the diode drop), frequency $2f$ = 100 Hz for 50 Hz mains.

**Derivation** (diode resistance $r_f$, load $R_L$, $\theta = \omega t$). In each half cycle one path conducts, so the load current is
$$i = I_m\sin\theta \ \ (0 \le \theta \le \pi), \qquad I_m = \frac{V_m}{r_f + R_L}$$
and the same hump repeats every $\pi$.

*DC (average) current:*
$$I_{dc} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{I_m}{\pi}\big[-\cos\theta\big]_0^{\pi} = \frac{2I_m}{\pi}$$
so $V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = \dfrac{2I_mR_L}{\pi} \approx \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}$ when $r_f \ll R_L$.

*RMS current:*
$$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta} = \sqrt{\frac{I_m^2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}} = \frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$$

*Efficiency:*
$$P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = \frac{4I_m^2}{\pi^2}R_L, \qquad P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(r_f + R_L) = \frac{I_m^2}{2}(r_f + R_L)$$
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{R_L}{r_f + R_L} = \frac{0.812}{1 + r_f/R_L}$$
**Maximum efficiency** (when $r_f \ll R_L$): $\mathbf{\eta_{max} = 81.2\%}$, twice the half-wave value of 40.6%.

## Part 2: Numerical (half-wave)

**Given:** $r_f = 25\ \Omega$, $R_L = 725\ \Omega$, $v = 60\sin\omega t$ so $V_m = 60$ V.

**(i) Currents**
$$I_{max} = \frac{V_m}{r_f + R_L} = \frac{60}{25 + 725} = \frac{60}{750} = \mathbf{80\ mA}$$
$$I_{dc} = \frac{I_{max}}{\pi} = \frac{80}{\pi} = \mathbf{25.46\ mA}, \qquad I_{rms} = \frac{I_{max}}{2} = \mathbf{40\ mA}$$

**(ii) DC output voltage**
$$V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = 0.02546 \times 725 = \mathbf{18.46\ V}$$

**(iii) Efficiency and ripple factor**
$$\eta = \frac{I_{dc}^2R_L}{I_{rms}^2(r_f + R_L)} = \frac{(0.02546)^2 \times 725}{(0.04)^2 \times 750} = \frac{0.470}{1.2} = \mathbf{39.2\%}$$
$$\gamma = \sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{rms}}{I_{dc}}\right)^2 - 1} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{40}{25.46}\right)^2 - 1} = \mathbf{1.21}$$

items.question_md: Differentiate between PNP and NPN transistors. Obtain Input/output & transfer characteristics of BJT in Common Collector (CC) configuration.
items.answer_md:
### PNP vs NPN
| Point | NPN | PNP |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | thin p-type base between n-type emitter and collector | thin n-type base between p-type emitter and collector |
| Majority carriers carrying current | electrons | holes |
| Biasing (active) | $V_{BE} > 0$, collector positive w.r.t. base | $V_{EB} > 0$, collector negative w.r.t. base |
| Conventional current | enters collector and base, leaves emitter | enters emitter, leaves base and collector |
| Symbol arrow on emitter | points outward | points inward |
| Speed | faster (electron mobility higher) | slower |

### CC configuration (emitter follower)
The collector is common to input and output: input between base and collector, output between emitter and collector. Circuit: $V_{BB}$ with rheostat drives the base, $V_{EE}$ supplies the emitter-collector circuit; meters for $I_B$, $I_E$, $V_{CB}$, $V_{CE}$.

**Input characteristics** ($I_B$ vs $V_{CB}$ at constant $V_{CE}$):
- Since $V_{BE} = V_{CE} - V_{CB}$, as $V_{CB}$ increases toward $V_{CE}$ the BE forward bias falls and $I_B$ decreases; the curve drops to zero when $V_{CB}$ approaches $V_{CE} - V_{BE(cut\text{-}in)}$.
- A higher $V_{CE}$ shifts the curve to the right. These curves are quite different from CE input curves.

**Output characteristics** ($I_E$ vs $V_{CE}$ at constant $I_B$):
- Nearly identical to the CE output curves because $I_E = I_C + I_B \approx I_C$: steep rise near the origin (saturation), then almost flat (active region), with $I_E = (1 + \beta)I_B$; the $I_B = 0$ curve marks cut-off.

**Transfer characteristics** ($I_E$ vs $I_B$ at constant $V_{CE}$):
- An almost straight line through the origin, slope $\gamma = \dfrac{\Delta I_E}{\Delta I_B} = 1 + \beta = \dfrac{1}{1 - \alpha}$, the CC current gain (high).

**Features of CC:** voltage gain slightly less than 1, no phase reversal, highest input resistance and lowest output resistance of the three configurations, so it is used as a buffer for impedance matching.

items.question_md:
Find the current in the $5\ \Omega$ resistor using Thevenin's theorem in Figure given below:

[Figure: Circuit with a 5 A current source (arrow up) on the left; in parallel, a branch of a $2\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a 10 V battery (+ on top); then a $10\ \Omega$ resistor branch; then a $5\ \Omega$ resistor branch on the right, all connected between top and bottom rails]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** between the top and bottom rails: 5 A source (up), 2 Ω + 10 V (+ top), 10 Ω, and the 5 Ω load.

**Step 1: Remove 5 Ω**, terminals = top and bottom rails.

**Step 2: $V_{th}$** (KCL at the top node):
$$5 = \frac{V_{th} - 10}{2} + \frac{V_{th}}{10} \Rightarrow V_{th}(0.5 + 0.1) = 5 + 5 \Rightarrow V_{th} = \frac{10}{0.6} = 16.67\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: $R_{th}$** (5 A opened, 10 V shorted):
$$R_{th} = 2 \parallel 10 = \frac{20}{12} = 1.667\ \Omega$$

**Step 4: Current in 5 Ω:**
$$I_5 = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + 5} = \frac{16.67}{6.667} = \mathbf{2.5\ A}\ \text{(downward)}$$

items.question_md:
Apply source transformation to find $v_x$ in the circuit of the given Fig.

[Figure: 50 V source (+ on top) in series with $10\ \Omega$ to node a; $40\ \Omega$ from node a to ground; $12\ \Omega$ between nodes a and b with $v_x$ across it (+ at a, − at b); from node b an 8 A current source (arrow up) to ground; from node b a $20\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a 40 V source (+ on top) to ground]
items.answer_md:
**Step 1: Left side.** 50 V in series with 10 Ω becomes a current source $50/10 = 5$ A in parallel with 10 Ω. This 10 Ω is in parallel with 40 Ω: $10 \parallel 40 = 8\ \Omega$. Convert back: $5 \times 8 = 40$ V in series with 8 Ω (+ at a).

**Step 2: Right side.** 40 V in series with 20 Ω becomes $40/20 = 2$ A (up into b) in parallel with 20 Ω. It adds to the 8 A source (also up into b): $8 + 2 = 10$ A in parallel with 20 Ω. Convert back: $10 \times 20 = 200$ V in series with 20 Ω (+ at b).

**Step 3: Single loop.** 40 V, 8 Ω, 12 Ω, 20 Ω, 200 V. Taking current $i$ from a to b through 12 Ω:
$$i = \frac{40 - 200}{8 + 12 + 20} = \frac{-160}{40} = -4\ \text{A}$$

**Step 4:**
$$v_x = 12\,i = 12 \times (-4) = \mathbf{-48\ V}$$
i.e. 4 A actually flows from b to a and node b is 48 V above node a.

Check by nodal analysis: $V_a = 72$ V, $V_b = 120$ V, $v_x = 72 - 120 = -48$ V.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Define active, reactive and apparent power in a single-phase AC circuit and deduce their relation using power triangle. State and explain the condition of resonance in a series R-L-C circuit.
items.answer_md:
**1. Active, reactive and apparent power**

With $v = V_m\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ (RMS $V$, $I$):
- **Active power** $P = VI\cos\phi$ (W): average power actually consumed.
- **Reactive power** $Q = VI\sin\phi$ (VAR): power exchanged back and forth with L/C fields; average zero.
- **Apparent power** $S = VI$ (VA): product of RMS voltage and current.

**2. Relation from the power triangle**

Resolve $I$ into $I\cos\phi$ (in phase with $V$) and $I\sin\phi$ ($90^\circ$ to $V$). Multiplying each side by $V$ gives a right triangle with base $P = VI\cos\phi$, height $Q = VI\sin\phi$ and hypotenuse $S = VI$, the angle between $P$ and $S$ being $\phi$:
$$\boxed{S = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}},\qquad \text{pf} = \cos\phi = \frac{P}{S},\qquad \tan\phi = \frac{Q}{P}$$

**3. Resonance in a series R-L-C circuit**

$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\qquad X_L = 2\pi fL,\ X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi fC}$$
**Condition:** the circuit is at resonance when the net reactance is zero:
$$X_L = X_C \;\Rightarrow\; 2\pi f_0L = \frac{1}{2\pi f_0C} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$
**Explanation (properties at resonance):**
- $Z = R$ (minimum), so current $I_0 = V/R$ is **maximum**.
- $V$ and $I$ are in phase, power factor = 1, $P = VI$.
- $V_L = V_C = I_0X_L$ are equal and opposite (cancel), and each can be many times $V$: $V_L/V = Q = \omega_0L/R$ (voltage magnification).
- Below $f_0$ the circuit is capacitive (leading pf), above $f_0$ inductive (lagging pf).

items.question_md: A resistance $R$, an inductance $L = 0.01\ H$ and a capacitance $C$ are connected in series. When an alternating voltage $v = 400\sin(300t - 20^\circ)$ is applied to the series combination, the current flowing is $10\sqrt{2}\sin(300t - 65^\circ)$. Find the values of $R$ and $C$.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $L = 0.01$ H, $v = 400\sin(300t - 20^\circ)$ V, $i = 10\sqrt2\sin(300t - 65^\circ)$ A, $\omega = 300$ rad/s.

**Impedance and phase:**
$$Z = \frac{V_m}{I_m} = \frac{400}{10\sqrt2} = 28.28\ \Omega,\qquad \phi = 65^\circ - 20^\circ = 45^\circ$$
**Resistance:**
$$R = Z\cos\phi = 28.28\cos45^\circ = \boxed{20\ \Omega}$$
**Net reactance:** $|X_L - X_C| = Z\sin45^\circ = 20\ \Omega$.

**Capacitance:** $X_L = \omega L = 300 \times 0.01 = 3\ \Omega$.

As printed, the current **lags** by $45^\circ$, which needs $X_L - X_C = +20\ \Omega$, i.e. $X_C = 3 - 20 = -17\ \Omega$: impossible, because $X_L$ is only 3 Ω. So with this L the net reactance must be capacitive, i.e. the current **leads** the voltage by $45^\circ$ (the intended current is $10\sqrt2\sin(300t + 25^\circ)$):
$$X_C - X_L = 20 \Rightarrow X_C = 3 + 20 = 23\ \Omega$$
$$C = \frac{1}{\omega X_C} = \frac{1}{300 \times 23} = \boxed{144.9\ \mu\text{F}}$$
Power factor $= \cos45^\circ = 0.707$ leading.

(In the textbook version of this problem $\omega = 3000$ rad/s: then $X_L = 30\ \Omega$, $X_C = 50\ \Omega$ and $C = 6.67\ \mu$F, with $R = 20\ \Omega$ as before.)

items.question_md:
What do you understand by self-excitation mode of DC machine?

A 230 V, 4-pole, wave-wound DC series motor has 782 conductors on its armature. It has armature and series field resistance of 0.75 ohm. The motor takes a current of 40 A. Estimate its speed if it has a flux per pole of 25 mWb
items.answer_md:
### Self-excitation
A DC machine is **self-excited** when its field winding is supplied from the machine's own armature instead of from a separate source. In a generator, the residual magnetism of the poles gives a small EMF when the armature is driven; this sends a small current through the field winding, which strengthens the flux (if the field is connected so that it aids the residual flux), raising the EMF further, until the voltage builds up to its working value. Conditions: residual magnetism must exist, the field must aid it, and the field circuit resistance must be below the critical resistance. Self-excited machines are classified by how the field is connected to the armature: **shunt** (field in parallel), **series** (field in series) and **compound** (both; short shunt or long shunt).

### Numerical
**Given:** $V = 230$ V; $P = 4$; wave winding so $A = 2$; $Z = 782$; $R_a + R_{se} = 0.75\ \Omega$; $I = I_a = I_{se} = 40$ A (series motor); $\Phi = 25$ mWb $= 0.025$ Wb.

**Step 1: Back EMF.**
$$E_b = V - I_a(R_a + R_{se}) = 230 - 40 \times 0.75 = 230 - 30 = 200\ \text{V}$$

**Step 2: Speed.**
$$N = \frac{60AE_b}{P\Phi Z} = \frac{60 \times 2 \times 200}{4 \times 0.025 \times 782} = \frac{24\,000}{78.2}$$

**Result:**
$$\boxed{N = 306.9\ \text{rpm} \approx 307\ \text{rpm}}$$

items.question_md: A six-pole lap-connected 230 V shunt motor has 410 armature conductors. It takes 41 A on full load. The flux per pole is 0.05 weber. The armature and field resistances are 0.1 ohm and 230 ohms respectively. Contact drop per brush = 1 V. Determine the speed of motor at full load.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $P = 6$; lap winding so $A = P = 6$; $V = 230$ V; $Z = 410$; $I_L = 41$ A; $\Phi = 0.05$ Wb; $R_a = 0.1\ \Omega$; $R_{sh} = 230\ \Omega$; contact drop $= 1$ V per brush.

**To find:** full-load speed $N$.

**Step 1: Armature current.** For a shunt motor, $I_a = I_L - I_{sh}$:
$$I_{sh} = \frac{V}{R_{sh}} = \frac{230}{230} = 1\ \text{A},\quad I_a = 41 - 1 = 40\ \text{A}$$

**Step 2: Back EMF** (two brushes in the current path, drop $= 2 \times 1 = 2$ V):
$$E_b = V - I_aR_a - V_{brush} = 230 - 40 \times 0.1 - 2 = 230 - 4 - 2 = 224\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: Speed.**
$$N = \frac{60AE_b}{P\Phi Z} = \frac{60 \times 6 \times 224}{6 \times 0.05 \times 410} = \frac{80\,640}{123}$$

**Result:**
$$\boxed{N = 655.6\ \text{rpm}}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: With the help of neat sketches explain the Core type and Shell type transformer. Discuss their advantages and disadvantages. Give the reasons for sandwich type of arrangement of windings.
items.answer_md:
**Core type** (sketch: a rectangular core with **two limbs**; the LV and HV windings are wound on the limbs, half of each winding on each limb, LV next to the core and HV outside it; the windings **surround the core**).
- Single magnetic circuit; flux path of one window around the core.
- Cylindrical (concentric) coils.

**Shell type** (sketch: a core with **three limbs**, the central limb twice as wide as the outer ones; both windings are on the central limb, interleaved as sandwich (disc) coils; the **core surrounds the windings**).
- Flux divides in the central limb and returns through the two outer limbs (double magnetic circuit).

| Feature | Core type | Shell type |
|---|---|---|
| Core surrounds windings? | No, windings surround core | Yes, core surrounds windings |
| Limbs | 2 | 3 (central limb carries winding) |
| Magnetic circuit | single | double (two parallel paths) |
| Windings | concentric cylindrical | sandwich / disc |
| Leakage reactance | higher | lower |
| Mechanical protection of winding | less | better (core shields winding) |
| Insulation, repair | easier to insulate and repair | difficult to inspect and repair |
| Cooling | better (more winding surface exposed) | poorer |
| Suitable for | high voltage, large ratings | low voltage, high current |

**Advantages and disadvantages**
- *Core type:* advantages: easy to assemble, insulate and repair; good natural cooling; suits high voltage. Disadvantages: larger leakage flux and reactance; less mechanical support to windings under short circuit.
- *Shell type:* advantages: lower leakage reactance; windings well supported and protected (withstand short-circuit forces); compact for low voltage high current. Disadvantages: difficult to dismantle and repair; poorer cooling; more iron.

**Reasons for sandwich (interleaved) arrangement of windings** (used in shell type: LV and HV disc coils alternated, with half-size LV coils at the top and bottom next to the yoke):
1. **Reduces leakage flux and leakage reactance**, because each HV coil sits between two LV coils and almost all the flux links both windings.
2. **Better voltage regulation** as a result of lower reactance.
3. The half LV coils at the ends lie next to the earthed core, which **reduces insulation requirement** (LV is easier to insulate from the core than HV).
4. Disc coils are mechanically strong against short-circuit forces and allow better oil circulation between coils.

items.question_md:
The O.C and S.C test data are given below for a single phase, 5 kVA, 200V/400V, 50 Hz transformer.

OC test data: 200 V, 1.25 A, 150 W

SC test data: 20 V, 12.5 A, 175 W

(i) Draw the equivalent circuit of the transformer
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 5 kVA, 200/400 V. OC test (LV, 200 V side): 200 V, 1.25 A, 150 W. SC test (HV side, rated HV current $= 5000/400 = 12.5$ A): 20 V, 12.5 A, 175 W.

**Shunt branch (from OC, referred to LV):**
$$\cos\phi_0 = \frac{150}{200 \times 1.25} = 0.6, \quad \sin\phi_0 = 0.8$$
$$I_w = 1.25 \times 0.6 = 0.75\ \text{A}, \quad I_\mu = 1.25 \times 0.8 = 1.0\ \text{A}$$
$$R_0 = \frac{200}{0.75} = 266.7\ \Omega, \quad X_0 = \frac{200}{1.0} = 200\ \Omega$$

**Series branch (from SC, referred to HV):**
$$Z_{eq} = \frac{20}{12.5} = 1.6\ \Omega, \quad R_{eq} = \frac{175}{12.5^2} = 1.12\ \Omega, \quad X_{eq} = \sqrt{1.6^2 - 1.12^2} = 1.143\ \Omega$$

Referred to the LV side ($\times (200/400)^2 = 0.25$): $R_{eq} = 0.28\ \Omega$, $X_{eq} = 0.2857\ \Omega$.

**Approximate equivalent circuit referred to LV (200 V) side:** across the 200 V input terminals the shunt branch $R_0 = 266.7\ \Omega$ in parallel with $X_0 = 200\ \Omega$ (carrying $I_w = 0.75$ A and $I_\mu = 1$ A, total $I_0 = 1.25$ A); then in series $R_{eq} = 0.28\ \Omega$ and $X_{eq} = 0.286\ \Omega$ leading to the output terminals and load $V_2'$ (ideal transformer of ratio 200/400 at the end if the HV load is shown).

items.question_md:
The O.C and S.C test data are given below for a single phase, 5 kVA, 200V/400V, 50 Hz transformer.

OC test data: 200 V, 1.25 A, 150 W

SC test data: 20 V, 12.5 A, 175 W

(ii) Determine the load at which the transformer operates at maximum efficiency
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 5 kVA, 200/400 V. Iron loss from OC test (rated voltage) $P_i = 150$ W. SC test current 12.5 A equals rated HV current ($5000/400 = 12.5$ A), so full-load copper loss $P_{cu,fl} = 175$ W.

**Condition:** maximum efficiency when copper loss = iron loss, i.e. $x^2P_{cu,fl} = P_i$:
$$x = \sqrt{\frac{P_i}{P_{cu,fl}}} = \sqrt{\frac{150}{175}} = 0.9258$$

**Load at maximum efficiency:**
$$\text{kVA} = x \times 5 = 0.9258 \times 5$$
$$\boxed{\approx 4.63\ \text{kVA}\ (92.6\%\ \text{of full load})}$$

The O.C and S.C test data are given below for a single phase, 5 kVA, 200V/400V, 50 Hz transformer.

OC test data: 200 V, 1.25 A, 150 W

SC test data: 20 V, 12.5 A, 175 W

(iii) Determine the maximum efficiency of transformer?
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 5 kVA; iron loss $P_i = 150$ W (OC test at rated 200 V); SC test at 12.5 A, which is rated HV current ($5000/400 = 12.5$ A), so $P_{cu,fl} = 175$ W.

**Load at maximum efficiency:**
$$x = \sqrt{\frac{P_i}{P_{cu,fl}}} = \sqrt{\frac{150}{175}} = 0.9258$$
$$\text{kVA} = 0.9258 \times 5 = 4.629\ \text{kVA}$$

At this load copper loss $= P_i = 150$ W, so total loss $= 300$ W.

**Maximum efficiency** (taking unity pf, at which efficiency is highest):
$$\eta_{max} = \frac{4629}{4629 + 300}\times 100$$
$$\boxed{\eta_{max} \approx 93.91\%}$$

(At 0.8 pf: $\eta_{max} = \dfrac{3703}{3703 + 300}\times 100 = 92.51\%$.)
