items.question_md: Compare Bridge type and center taped type of full wave rectifier. A half wave rectifier using silicon diode has a secondary emf of 10 V (Peak) with a resistance of $0.2\ \Omega$. The diode has a forward resistance of $0.05\ \Omega$ and a threshold voltage of 0.7V. If load resistance is $500\ \Omega$, determine (i) dc load current (ii) dc load voltage (iii) Efficiency (iv) Ripple Factor
items.answer_md:
## Part 1: Bridge vs centre-tap full-wave rectifier

| Point | Centre-tap | Bridge |
|---|---|---|
| Number of diodes | 2 | 4 |
| Transformer | Centre-tapped needed | Ordinary, no centre tap |
| PIV per diode | $2V_m$ | $V_m$ |
| $V_{dc}$ (same secondary voltage) | $2V_m'/\pi$ with $V_m'$ = half the secondary | $2V_m/\pi$ with full secondary, so double |
| TUF | 0.693 | 0.812 |
| Diode drops in conduction path | One ($V_\gamma$) | Two ($2V_\gamma$) |
| Efficiency (max), ripple factor | 81.2%, 0.482 | 81.2%, 0.482 |
| Suitability | Low-voltage outputs | Most common; preferred |

## Part 2: Numerical (half-wave)

**Given:** $V_m = 10$ V (peak), $R_s = 0.2\ \Omega$, $r_f = 0.05\ \Omega$, $V_\gamma = 0.7$ V, $R_L = 500\ \Omega$.

**Peak current:**
$$I_m = \frac{V_m - V_\gamma}{R_s + r_f + R_L} = \frac{10 - 0.7}{0.2 + 0.05 + 500} = \frac{9.3}{500.25} = 18.59\ \text{mA}$$

**(i) DC load current**
$$I_{dc} = \frac{I_m}{\pi} = \frac{18.59}{\pi} = \mathbf{5.92\ mA}$$

**(ii) DC load voltage**
$$V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = 0.005918 \times 500 = \mathbf{2.96\ V}$$

**(iii) Efficiency**
- $P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = (0.005918)^2 \times 500 = 17.51$ mW
- $I_{rms} = I_m/2 = 9.295$ mA
- $P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(R_s + r_f + R_L) + V_\gamma I_{dc} = 43.22 + 4.14 = 47.37$ mW
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{17.51}{47.37} = \mathbf{37.0\%}$$

**(iv) Ripple factor** (half wave):
$$\gamma = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 - 1} = \mathbf{1.21}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Differentiate between p-n-p and n-p-n type transistors and explain the working of n-p-n type transistor. Draw and discuss the input and output characteristics of a CE transistor & indicate therein the active, cut-off and saturation region.
items.answer_md:
### p-n-p vs n-p-n
| Point | NPN | PNP |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | thin p-type base between n-type emitter and collector | thin n-type base between p-type emitter and collector |
| Majority carriers carrying current | electrons | holes |
| Biasing (active) | $V_{BE} > 0$, collector positive w.r.t. base | $V_{EB} > 0$, collector negative w.r.t. base |
| Conventional current | enters collector and base, leaves emitter | enters emitter, leaves base and collector |
| Symbol arrow on emitter | points outward | points inward |
| Speed | faster (electron mobility higher) | slower |

### Working of an n-p-n transistor
- Emitter-base junction is **forward biased** ($V_{BE} \approx 0.7$ V for Si); collector-base junction is **reverse biased** ($V_{CC}$).
- The heavily doped n-type emitter injects a large number of electrons into the base; this is the emitter current $I_E$.
- The base is thin and lightly doped, so only a few electrons (about 2 to 5%) recombine with holes there; this forms the small base current $I_B$.
- The remaining electrons (95 to 98%) diffuse across the base and are swept into the collector by the strong field of the reverse-biased CB junction, forming $I_C$.
- Hence $I_E = I_B + I_C$, $I_C = \alpha I_E + I_{CBO}$, and a small change in $I_B$ controls a large $I_C = \beta I_B$, which is the basis of amplification.

### CE characteristics
**Input characteristics** ($I_B$ vs $V_{BE}$ at constant $V_{CE}$). Circuit: base supply $V_{BB}$ through a rheostat, collector supply $V_{CC}$, ammeters for $I_B$ (μA) and $I_C$ (mA), voltmeters for $V_{BE}$ and $V_{CE}$.
- The curve is like a forward-biased diode: $I_B \approx 0$ until $V_{BE}$ reaches the cut-in voltage (about 0.5 to 0.7 V for Si), then rises steeply.
- Increasing $V_{CE}$ shifts the curve slightly to the **right** (less $I_B$ for the same $V_{BE}$), because the wider collector depletion region narrows the base (Early effect) and less recombination occurs in the base.
- Input resistance $r_i = \dfrac{\Delta V_{BE}}{\Delta I_B}\Big|_{V_{CE}}$, typically about 1 kΩ (low).

**Output characteristics** ($I_C$ vs $V_{CE}$ at constant $I_B$, a family of curves for $I_B = 0, 20, 40, 60\ \mu A, \dots$):
- For each $I_B$, $I_C$ rises steeply for very small $V_{CE}$ (0 to about 0.2 to 0.3 V) and then becomes almost flat, rising only slightly with $V_{CE}$ (Early effect).
- In the flat portion $I_C \approx \beta I_B$; higher $I_B$ gives a higher curve.
- Output resistance $r_o = \dfrac{\Delta V_{CE}}{\Delta I_C}\Big|_{I_B}$ (high, tens of kΩ); current gain $\beta = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}\Big|_{V_{CE}}$ (50 to 300).

**Regions (mark them on the output graph):**
| Region | Where on the graph | Junction bias | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active | flat part of the curves, above $I_B = 0$ and right of the knee | BE forward, CB reverse | amplifier |
| Saturation | steep rising part near the vertical axis, $V_{CE} \le V_{CE(sat)} \approx 0.2$ V | both junctions forward | switch ON |
| Cut-off | below the $I_B = 0$ curve, $I_C = I_{CEO}$ (small, not exactly 0) | both junctions reverse (or BE not forward) | switch OFF |

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/End Term/End Term Sem 1 2025-26.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the relation between the voltage and current for an R-L-C circuit using phasor diagram. Also derive the average power consumed by the circuit. Define and explain the condition of Series resonance.
items.answer_md:
**1. Voltage-current relation using the phasor diagram**

In a series R-L-C circuit carrying current $I$ (RMS), the current is common, so take $\bar I$ as the reference phasor.
- $V_R = IR$, in phase with $I$
- $V_L = IX_L$, leading $I$ by $90^\circ$, $X_L = 2\pi fL$
- $V_C = IX_C$, lagging $I$ by $90^\circ$, $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$

$V_L$ and $V_C$ are in direct opposition, so their resultant is $(V_L - V_C)$ (taking $X_L > X_C$). The supply voltage is the phasor sum:
$$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$
$$\boxed{I = \frac{V}{Z}},\qquad Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$
Phasor diagram (in words): $I$ horizontal, $V_R$ along it, $V_L$ up, $V_C$ down; $V$ is the hypotenuse of $V_R$ and $(V_L - V_C)$, at angle $\phi$ above $I$. In complex form $\bar Z = R + j(X_L - X_C)$.
- $X_L > X_C$: current lags $V$ by $\phi$ (inductive)
- $X_L < X_C$: current leads $V$ (capacitive)
- $X_L = X_C$: in phase (resonance)

**2. Average power**

Let $v = V_m\sin\omega t$, $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$.
$$p = vi = V_mI_m\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$
The second term averages to zero over a cycle:
$$P = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\phi = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}\cos\phi$$
$$\boxed{P = VI\cos\phi = I^2R\ \text{W}}$$
since $\cos\phi = R/Z$ and $V = IZ$. Only R consumes power; L and C only exchange energy.

**3. Series resonance**

**Definition:** a series R-L-C circuit is at resonance when its net reactance is zero, $X_L = X_C$, so that voltage and current are in phase:
$$2\pi f_0L = \frac{1}{2\pi f_0C} \Rightarrow \boxed{f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$
**At resonance:**
- $Z = R$ (minimum); current $I_0 = V/R$ is maximum
- power factor = 1, $P = VI$
- $V_L = V_C = I_0X_L$, equal and opposite; each equals $QV$ where $Q = \omega_0L/R$ (voltage magnification), so each can exceed $V$
- below $f_0$ the circuit is capacitive, above $f_0$ inductive
- it is called an **acceptor circuit**, since it accepts (passes maximum current at) $f_0$.

items.question_md:
In the arrangement shown in given fig. C has a capacitance of $20\ \mu F$ and the current flowing through the circuit is $0.345\ A$. If the voltages are as indicated, find (i) the frequency (ii) loss in the iron-cored inductor and (iii) the applied voltage.

[Figure: Series circuit of resistor R, iron-cored inductor L and capacitor C across an AC source, with $I = 0.345\ A$. Voltage across R = 25 V, across L = 40 V, across C = 55 V, and across R and L together = 50 V.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $C = 20\ \mu$F, $I = 0.345$ A, $V_R = 25$ V, $V_{coil} = 40$ V, $V_C = 55$ V, $V_{R+coil} = 50$ V.

Since $25 + 40 \neq 50$, the iron-cored coil has a loss component $V_r$ (in phase with $I$) and a reactive component $V_X$ (leading $I$ by $90^\circ$).

**(i) Frequency**
$$X_C = \frac{V_C}{I} = \frac{55}{0.345} = 159.42\ \Omega$$
$$f = \frac{1}{2\pi CX_C} = \frac{1}{2\pi(20\times10^{-6})(159.42)} = \boxed{49.9 \approx 50\ \text{Hz}}$$

**(ii) Loss in the iron-cored inductor**
$$V_r^2 + V_X^2 = 40^2\quad(1),\qquad (25 + V_r)^2 + V_X^2 = 50^2\quad(2)$$
(2) minus (1): $625 + 50V_r = 2500 - 1600 = 900$
$$V_r = 5.5\ \text{V},\qquad V_X = \sqrt{40^2 - 5.5^2} = 39.62\ \text{V}$$
$$P_{coil} = V_rI = 5.5 \times 0.345 = \boxed{1.90\ \text{W}}$$

**(iii) Applied voltage**
$$V = \sqrt{(V_R + V_r)^2 + (V_X - V_C)^2} = \sqrt{30.5^2 + (39.62 - 55)^2} = \sqrt{930.25 + 236.5}$$
$$\boxed{V = 34.16\ \text{V}}$$
Power factor $= 30.5/34.16 = 0.893$ leading (since $V_C > V_X$).

items.question_md:
Determine $R_L$ in figure for maximum power transfer to the load.

[Figure: Ladder network fed by a 20 V source. Series arm resistors from left to right: 1 Ω, 21 Ω, 3 Ω, 6 Ω leading to terminal A. Shunt branches: 21 Ω after the 1 Ω; 21 Ω after the 21 Ω; 6 Ω after the 3 Ω; 6 Ω after the 6 Ω. A 5 Ω resistor is in the common return path below the first two shunt branches. Load $R_L$ is connected between terminals A and B.]
items.answer_md:
**Principle:** By the maximum power transfer theorem, $R_L = R_{th}$, the resistance seen from A-B with the 20 V source replaced by a short.

**Reading of the figure:** top nodes $n_1$ (after 1 Ω), $n_2$ (after 21 Ω), $n_3$ (after 3 Ω), A (after 6 Ω). The two 21 Ω shunts return to a node x, and the common return resistor 5 Ω joins x to the main bottom rail (B, source negative). The 6 Ω shunts go from $n_3$ and A to B.

**Step 1: Kill the source.** 20 V shorted, so $n_1$ is joined to B through 1 Ω.

**Step 2: Reduce the left part by delta-star.** $n_1$, $n_2$, x form a delta of three 21 Ω resistors. Converting to star (equal arms, $R_Y = R_\Delta/3$): each arm $= 7\ \Omega$, meeting at star point S.
- Path S to B via $n_1$: $7 + 1 = 8\ \Omega$
- Path S to B via x: $7 + 5 = 12\ \Omega$
- These are in parallel: $8 \parallel 12 = 4.8\ \Omega$
- Add the arm to $n_2$: $R_{n_2B} = 7 + 4.8 = 11.8\ \Omega$

**Step 3: Reduce towards A-B.**
$$R_1 = 11.8 + 3 = 14.8\ \Omega,\quad R_2 = 14.8 \parallel 6 = 4.269\ \Omega$$
$$R_3 = 4.269 + 6 = 10.269\ \Omega,\quad R_{th} = 10.269 \parallel 6 = \frac{178}{47} = 3.79\ \Omega$$

**Result:**
$$\boxed{R_L = R_{th} \approx 3.79\ \Omega}$$

For completeness, the open-circuit voltage on this reading is $V_{th} = 60/47 = 1.28$ V, so $P_{max} = V_{th}^2/(4R_{th}) = 0.108$ W.

Note: the answer depends on exactly where the 5 Ω sits in the return path; the method (short the source, reduce towards A-B, set $R_L = R_{th}$) is the same for any reading.

items.question_md:
Find the current through the $5\ \Omega$ resistor using Thevenin's theorem in the given figure

[Figure: Three parallel branches between a top node and a bottom node. Left branch: 3 Ω in series with a 20 V source. Middle branch: 8 Ω in series with a 10 V source. Right branch: 5 Ω, connected to the top node through a 3 Ω resistor.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** branches between top node T and bottom node: 3 Ω + 20 V, 8 Ω + 10 V (both + at top), and 3 Ω + 5 Ω (load).

**Step 1: Remove 5 Ω.** No current in the series 3 Ω, so $V_{th} = V_T$.

**Step 2: $V_{th}$ (KCL at T):**
$$\frac{V_T - 20}{3} + \frac{V_T - 10}{8} = 0 \Rightarrow V_T = \frac{20/3 + 10/8}{1/3 + 1/8} = \frac{7.917}{0.4583} = 17.27\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: $R_{th}$** (sources shorted):
$$R_{th} = (3 \parallel 8) + 3 = 2.182 + 3 = 5.182\ \Omega$$

**Step 4: Load current:**
$$I_5 = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + 5} = \frac{17.27}{10.18} = \mathbf{1.70\ A}$$
flowing downward through the 5 Ω.

items.question_md: Give the classification of Transformers. With the help of neat sketches explain the Core type and Shell type transformer. Discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
items.answer_md:
**Classification of transformers**
1. **By construction:** core type, shell type, berry (spiral core) type.
2. **By voltage change:** step-up ($N_2 > N_1$), step-down ($N_2 < N_1$), isolation (1:1).
3. **By number of phases:** single-phase, three-phase.
4. **By application:** power transformer, distribution transformer, instrument transformers (CT, PT), auto-transformer.
5. **By cooling:** air-cooled (dry type), oil-immersed natural cooled (ONAN), oil-immersed forced-air (ONAF), forced oil (OFAF), water-cooled.
6. **By core material:** iron-core, air-core, ferrite-core.

**Core type** (sketch: a rectangular core with **two limbs**; the LV and HV windings are wound on the limbs, half of each winding on each limb, LV next to the core and HV outside it; the windings **surround the core**).
- Single magnetic circuit; flux path of one window around the core.
- Cylindrical (concentric) coils.

**Shell type** (sketch: a core with **three limbs**, the central limb twice as wide as the outer ones; both windings are on the central limb, interleaved as sandwich (disc) coils; the **core surrounds the windings**).
- Flux divides in the central limb and returns through the two outer limbs (double magnetic circuit).

| Feature | Core type | Shell type |
|---|---|---|
| Core surrounds windings? | No, windings surround core | Yes, core surrounds windings |
| Limbs | 2 | 3 (central limb carries winding) |
| Magnetic circuit | single | double (two parallel paths) |
| Windings | concentric cylindrical | sandwich / disc |
| Leakage reactance | higher | lower |
| Mechanical protection of winding | less | better (core shields winding) |
| Insulation, repair | easier to insulate and repair | difficult to inspect and repair |
| Cooling | better (more winding surface exposed) | poorer |
| Suitable for | high voltage, large ratings | low voltage, high current |

**Advantages and disadvantages**
- *Core type:* advantages: easy to assemble, insulate and repair; good natural cooling; suits high voltage. Disadvantages: larger leakage flux and reactance; less mechanical support to windings under short circuit.
- *Shell type:* advantages: lower leakage reactance; windings well supported and protected (withstand short-circuit forces); compact for low voltage high current. Disadvantages: difficult to dismantle and repair; poorer cooling; more iron.

items.question_md:
A 4 kVA, 400/200 V, 50 Hz 1-$\Phi$ transformer has the following test data:

O.C. test (l.v. side) - 200 V, 1 A, 64 W

S.C. test (h.v. side) - 15 V, 10 A, 80 W

Determine:

(i) Equivalent circuit referred to l.v. side, and

(ii) Secondary load voltage on full load at 0.8 power factor lagging
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 4 kVA, 400/200 V. OC (LV): $V_0 = 200$ V, $I_0 = 1$ A, $P_0 = 64$ W. SC (HV): $V_{sc} = 15$ V, $I_{sc} = 10$ A, $P_{sc} = 80$ W. Rated HV current $= 4000/400 = 10$ A, so the SC test is at rated current. $K = N_2/N_1 = 200/400 = 0.5$ (secondary = LV).

**(i) Equivalent circuit referred to LV side**

*Shunt branch (OC test, already on LV):*
$$\cos\phi_0 = \frac{P_0}{V_0I_0} = \frac{64}{200 \times 1} = 0.32, \quad \sin\phi_0 = 0.9474$$
$$I_w = I_0\cos\phi_0 = 0.32\ \text{A}, \quad I_\mu = I_0\sin\phi_0 = 0.9474\ \text{A}$$
$$R_0 = \frac{V_0}{I_w} = \frac{200}{0.32} = 625\ \Omega, \quad X_0 = \frac{V_0}{I_\mu} = \frac{200}{0.9474} = 211.1\ \Omega$$

*Series branch (SC test, on HV):*
$$Z_{01} = \frac{15}{10} = 1.5\ \Omega, \quad R_{01} = \frac{80}{10^2} = 0.8\ \Omega, \quad X_{01} = \sqrt{1.5^2 - 0.8^2} = 1.269\ \Omega$$

*Referred to LV* (multiply by $K^2 = 0.25$):
$$R_{02} = 0.2\ \Omega, \quad X_{02} = 0.3172\ \Omega, \quad Z_{02} = 0.375\ \Omega$$

**Equivalent circuit (LV side):** supply terminals with the shunt branch $R_0 = 625\ \Omega \parallel X_0 = 211.1\ \Omega$ across them, followed by series $R_{02} = 0.2\ \Omega$ and $X_{02} = 0.317\ \Omega$ to the load terminals.

**(ii) Secondary voltage on full load, 0.8 pf lagging**
$$I_2 = \frac{4000}{200} = 20\ \text{A}, \quad \cos\phi = 0.8, \ \sin\phi = 0.6$$
$$\text{Drop} = I_2(R_{02}\cos\phi + X_{02}\sin\phi) = 20(0.2 \times 0.8 + 0.3172 \times 0.6) = 7.01\ \text{V}$$
$$V_2 = 200 - 7.01$$

**Result:** $V_2 \approx$ **192.99 V** (regulation $= 7.01/200 = 3.50\%$)

items.question_md: Mention a few applications of a BJT. Explain the input and output characteristics of an NPN transistor (with the base terminal common to both input and output) with neat diagrams.
items.answer_md:
### Applications of a BJT
- Amplifier (audio, RF, small-signal voltage and power amplifiers)
- Electronic switch (ON in saturation, OFF in cut-off), digital logic gates
- Oscillators, voltage regulators (series pass element), current sources, buffers and impedance matching

### CB configuration (NPN)
Base common to input and output; input applied between emitter and base ($V_{EB}$, current $I_E$), output taken between collector and base ($V_{CB}$, current $I_C$). Circuit: $V_{EE}$ forward-biases the emitter-base junction through a rheostat, $V_{CC}$ reverse-biases the collector-base junction; ammeters in emitter and collector leads, voltmeters across EB and CB.

### Input characteristics ($I_E$ vs $V_{EB}$ at constant $V_{CB}$)
- Similar to a forward-biased diode: negligible $I_E$ below the cut-in voltage (about 0.5 to 0.7 V for Si), then $I_E$ rises rapidly.
- Increasing $V_{CB}$ shifts the curve to the **left** (more $I_E$ at a given $V_{EB}$), due to base-width modulation (Early effect).
- Input resistance $r_i = \dfrac{\Delta V_{EB}}{\Delta I_E}\Big|_{V_{CB}}$ is very low (tens of ohms).

### Output characteristics ($I_C$ vs $V_{CB}$ at constant $I_E$, curves for $I_E = 0, 1, 2, 3$ mA, ...)
- **Active region** (right of the vertical axis, $V_{CB} > 0$): $I_C \approx \alpha I_E$, nearly equal to $I_E$ and almost independent of $V_{CB}$; the curves are nearly horizontal. Output resistance $r_o = \dfrac{\Delta V_{CB}}{\Delta I_C}\Big|_{I_E}$ is very high (MΩ).
- **Saturation region** (left of the vertical axis, small negative $V_{CB}$): the CB junction becomes forward biased and $I_C$ falls rapidly to zero.
- **Cut-off region** (along the $I_E = 0$ curve): only the small reverse leakage $I_C = I_{CBO}$ flows.
- Current gain $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_E}\Big|_{V_{CB}}$ is slightly **less than 1** (0.95 to 0.995).

items.topic: Half wave and full wave rectifiers
items.question_md:
A Half wave rectifier has a secondary emf of 10V (rms) with winding resistance of transformer is $0.5\ \Omega$. The silicon diode has a forward resistance of $15\ \Omega$. If load resistance is $300\ \Omega$, determine

(i) DC load current (ii) DC load voltage (iii) Efficiency (iv) Ripple Factor
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $E_{s,rms} = 10$ V, $R_s = 0.5\ \Omega$, $r_f = 15\ \Omega$, $R_L = 300\ \Omega$, half-wave. No cut-in voltage is given, so the diode is modelled by $r_f$ alone.

**Peak secondary voltage:** $V_m = \sqrt2 \times 10 = 14.142$ V

**Peak current:**
$$I_m = \frac{V_m}{R_s + r_f + R_L} = \frac{14.142}{0.5 + 15 + 300} = \frac{14.142}{315.5} = 0.04482\ \text{A} = 44.82\ \text{mA}$$

**(i) DC load current**
$$I_{dc} = \frac{I_m}{\pi} = \frac{44.82}{\pi} = \mathbf{14.27\ mA}$$

**(ii) DC load voltage**
$$V_{dc} = I_{dc}R_L = 0.01427 \times 300 = \mathbf{4.28\ V}$$

**(iii) Efficiency**, with $I_{rms} = I_m/2$:
$$\eta = \frac{I_{dc}^2R_L}{I_{rms}^2(R_s + r_f + R_L)} = \frac{0.406}{1 + \dfrac{R_s + r_f}{R_L}} = \frac{0.406}{1 + \dfrac{15.5}{300}} = \mathbf{0.385 = 38.5\%}$$

**(iv) Ripple factor** (half-wave, $I_{rms}/I_{dc} = \pi/2$):
$$\gamma = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 - 1} = \mathbf{1.21}$$

The ripple factor does not depend on the resistances; it is fixed by the waveform shape.

items.question_md:
For the network shown in Fig.1 determine the currents in each of the resistors using mesh analysis.

[Figure: Fig.1 – A 54 V battery supplies a current $I = 8$ A into the top node of a bridge network. The battery's other terminal connects to the bottom node. Resistors: 2 Ω between the top node and the left node, 14 Ω between the top node and the right node, 32 Ω between the left node and the right node, 11 Ω between the left node and the bottom node, and 3 Ω between the right node and the bottom node.]
items.answer_md:
**Set-up:** nodes T (top), L (left), R (right), Bt (bottom). Mesh currents, all clockwise:
- $I_1$: battery → T → 2 Ω → L → 11 Ω → Bt → battery (this is the battery current, $I_1 = 8$ A)
- $I_2$: T → 14 Ω → R → 32 Ω → L → 2 Ω → T
- $I_3$: L → 32 Ω → R → 3 Ω → Bt → 11 Ω → L

**Mesh equations**
- Mesh 1: $54 = 13I_1 - 2I_2 - 11I_3$
- Mesh 2: $0 = -2I_1 + 48I_2 - 32I_3$
- Mesh 3: $0 = -11I_1 - 32I_2 + 46I_3$

**Solving** (Cramer's rule or elimination):
$$I_1 = 8\ \text{A},\quad I_2 = 3\ \text{A},\quad I_3 = 4\ \text{A}$$
$I_1 = 8$ A agrees with the given battery current ($R_{eq} = 54/8 = 6.75\ \Omega$).

**Current in each resistor**
| Resistor | Current | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Ω | $I_1 - I_2 = 5$ A | T to L |
| 14 Ω | $I_2 = 3$ A | T to R |
| 32 Ω | $I_3 - I_2 = 1$ A | L to R |
| 11 Ω | $I_1 - I_3 = 4$ A | L to Bt |
| 3 Ω | $I_3 = 4$ A | R to Bt |

**Check:** $V_L = 54 - 2(5) = 44$ V, $V_R = 54 - 14(3) = 12$ V; $11\ \Omega$: $44/11 = 4$ A ✓, $3\ \Omega$: $12/3 = 4$ A ✓, $32\ \Omega$: $(44 - 12)/32 = 1$ A ✓.

items.question_md: An alternating voltage is given by $v = 282.8 \sin 314t$ volts. Find (c) the instantaneous value of voltage when $t = 4$ ms.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $v = 282.8\sin314t$ V, $t = 4$ ms $= 0.004$ s.

$$\omega t = 314\times0.004 = 1.256\ \text{rad}\ (= 71.96^\circ)$$
$$v = 282.8\sin(1.256\ \text{rad}) = 282.8\times0.9510 = \mathbf{268.9\ V}$$

items.question_md: A coil having a resistance of $10\ \Omega$ and an inductance of $125$ mH is connected in series with a $60\ \mu F$ capacitor across a $120$ V supply. At what frequency does resonance occurs? Find the current flowing at the resonant frequency.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $R = 10\ \Omega$, $L = 125$ mH $= 0.125$ H, $C = 60\ \mu$F $= 60\times10^{-6}$ F, $V = 120$ V.

**Resonant frequency:**
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{0.125 \times 60\times10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{7.5\times10^{-6}}}$$
$$\boxed{f_0 = 58.12\ \text{Hz}}$$

**Current at resonance:** $X_L = X_C$, so $Z = R = 10\ \Omega$:
$$I_0 = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{120}{10} = \boxed{12\ \text{A}}$$
in phase with the supply voltage (unity power factor). ($X_L = X_C = 45.64\ \Omega$ at $f_0$.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2021.pdf
items.question_md: A star-connected load consists of three identical coils each of resistance $30\ \Omega$ and inductance $127.3$ mH. If the line current is $5.08$ A, calculate the line voltage if the supply frequency is $50$ Hz.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** star connection, per phase $R = 30\ \Omega$, $L = 127.3$ mH; $I_L = 5.08$ A; $f = 50$ Hz.

**Per-phase impedance**
$$X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi(50)(0.1273) = 39.99 \approx 40\ \Omega$$
$$Z_{ph} = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\ \Omega$$

**Phase voltage** (in star, $I_{ph} = I_L = 5.08$ A):
$$V_{ph} = I_{ph}Z_{ph} = 5.08\times50 = 254\ \text{V}$$

**Line voltage** (in star, $V_L = \sqrt3V_{ph}$):
$$V_L = \sqrt3\times254 = \mathbf{439.9\ V \approx 440\ V}$$
(Power factor $= R/Z = 30/50 = 0.6$ lagging.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md:
Maximum value of sinusoidal alternating voltage and current are 400V and 20 amps respectively to a circuit connected to 50 Hz supply. Instantaneous values of voltage and currents are 283 V and 10 amp respectively at time $t=0$ both increasing positively.

(i) Write down expression for voltage and current at time t
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $V_m = 400$ V, $I_m = 20$ A, $f = 50$ Hz, $v(0) = 283$ V, $i(0) = 10$ A, both increasing.

$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(50) = 314.16$ rad/s

Let $v = V_m\sin(\omega t + \theta_v)$ and $i = I_m\sin(\omega t + \theta_i)$.

At $t = 0$:
$$\sin\theta_v = \frac{283}{400} = 0.7075 \Rightarrow \theta_v = 45.03^\circ \approx 45^\circ$$
$$\sin\theta_i = \frac{10}{20} = 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta_i = 30^\circ$$
Both quantities are increasing positively at $t = 0$, so the angles lie in the first quadrant (not $135^\circ$ or $150^\circ$).

$$\boxed{v = 400\sin(314.16t + 45^\circ)\ \text{V}},\qquad \boxed{i = 20\sin(314.16t + 30^\circ)\ \text{A}}$$

The current lags the voltage by $45^\circ - 30^\circ = 15^\circ$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md:
Maximum value of sinusoidal alternating voltage and current are 400V and 20 amps respectively to a circuit connected to 50 Hz supply. Instantaneous values of voltage and currents are 283 V and 10 amp respectively at time $t=0$ both increasing positively.

(ii) Determine power consume in the circuit.
items.answer_md:
From part (i): $v = 400\sin(\omega t + 45^\circ)$ V and $i = 20\sin(\omega t + 30^\circ)$ A, so the current lags the voltage by $\phi = 45^\circ - 30^\circ = 15^\circ$.

$$P = VI\cos\phi = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}\cos\phi = \frac{400 \times 20}{2}\cos15^\circ$$
$$P = 4000 \times 0.9659 = \boxed{3863.7\ \text{W} \approx 3.86\ \text{kW}}$$
Power factor $= \cos15^\circ = 0.966$ lagging.

items.question_md:
A 50 Hz alternating current $i = 1.414 \sin(\omega t)$ amp is passed through a series circuit consisting resistance of 100 ohm and inductance of 0.3183 Henry.

Find the expression for instantaneous value of voltage across (i) resistance
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $i = 1.414\sin\omega t$ A, $f = 50$ Hz so $\omega = 2\pi(50) = 314.16$ rad/s; $R = 100\ \Omega$.

Voltage across a resistance is in phase with the current:
$$v_R = iR = 1.414\times100\sin\omega t$$
$$\boxed{v_R = 141.4\sin(314.16t)\ \text{V}}$$
(rms value $= 100$ V.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md:
A 50 Hz alternating current $i = 1.414 \sin(\omega t)$ amp is passed through a series circuit consisting resistance of 100 ohm and inductance of 0.3183 Henry.

Find the expression for instantaneous value of voltage across (ii) inductance
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $i = 1.414\sin\omega t$ A, $\omega = 2\pi(50) = 314.16$ rad/s, $L = 0.3183$ H.

$$X_L = \omega L = 314.16\times0.3183 = 100\ \Omega$$
The voltage across an inductance leads the current by 90°:
$$v_L = I_mX_L\sin(\omega t + 90^\circ) = 1.414\times100\sin(\omega t + 90^\circ)$$
$$\boxed{v_L = 141.4\sin(314.16t + \pi/2)\ \text{V} = 141.4\cos(314.16t)\ \text{V}}$$
(Equivalently $v_L = L\,di/dt = 0.3183\times1.414\times314.16\cos\omega t$.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md:
A 50 Hz alternating current $i = 1.414 \sin(\omega t)$ amp is passed through a series circuit consisting resistance of 100 ohm and inductance of 0.3183 Henry.

Find the expression for instantaneous value of voltage across (iii) combination
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $i = 1.414\sin\omega t$ A, $\omega = 314.16$ rad/s, $R = 100\ \Omega$, $X_L = \omega L = 314.16\times0.3183 = 100\ \Omega$.

$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{100^2 + 100^2} = 141.42\ \Omega,\qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L}{R} = 45^\circ$$
$$V_m = I_mZ = 1.414\times141.42 = 200\ \text{V}$$
The combined voltage leads the current by 45°:
$$\boxed{v = 200\sin(314.16t + \pi/4)\ \text{V}}$$
Check: $v_R + v_L = 141.4\sin\omega t + 141.4\cos\omega t = 200\sin(\omega t + 45^\circ)$.

items.question_md: Derive an expression for power in a 3-phase star-connected system in terms of (*i*) phase values of voltages and currents.
items.answer_md:
**Star-connected balanced load, power in terms of phase values**

Let the phase voltage be $V_{ph}$, phase current $I_{ph}$, and $\phi$ the angle by which each phase current lags its phase voltage.

Taking phase R as reference:
$$v_R = \sqrt2V_{ph}\sin\omega t,\quad i_R = \sqrt2I_{ph}\sin(\omega t - \phi)$$
and the other two phases displaced by $120^\circ$ and $240^\circ$.

Power in one phase (average):
$$P_{ph} = V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi$$
(the instantaneous product $v_Ri_R = V_{ph}I_{ph}[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)]$, whose second term averages to zero).

For a balanced system all three phases take equal power, so the total power is
$$\boxed{P = 3V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi\ \text{W}}$$
(Also, the double-frequency terms of the three phases are $120^\circ$ apart and sum to zero, so the total instantaneous three-phase power is constant and equal to $3V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi$.)

Similarly $Q = 3V_{ph}I_{ph}\sin\phi$ VAR and $S = 3V_{ph}I_{ph}$ VA.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md: Derive an expression for power in a 3-phase star-connected system in terms of (*ii*) line values of voltages and currents.
items.answer_md:
**Star-connected balanced load, power in terms of line values**

Start from the per-phase result:
$$P = 3V_{ph}I_{ph}\cos\phi$$

In a star connection:
- the line current equals the phase current: $I_L = I_{ph}$
- the line voltage is the phasor difference of two phase voltages $120^\circ$ apart: $\bar V_{RY} = \bar V_R - \bar V_Y$, whose magnitude is $2V_{ph}\cos30^\circ = \sqrt3V_{ph}$, so $V_L = \sqrt3V_{ph}$ (leading the phase voltage by $30^\circ$).

Substituting $V_{ph} = V_L/\sqrt3$ and $I_{ph} = I_L$:
$$P = 3\cdot\frac{V_L}{\sqrt3}\cdot I_L\cos\phi$$
$$\boxed{P = \sqrt3V_LI_L\cos\phi\ \text{W}}$$
where $\phi$ is still the angle between **phase** voltage and **phase** current (not between line voltage and line current).

Likewise $Q = \sqrt3V_LI_L\sin\phi$ VAR and $S = \sqrt3V_LI_L$ VA.

items.question_md: Define the following term: (i) Residual magnetism
items.answer_md: **Residual magnetism:** the magnetism (flux density) that **remains in a ferromagnetic material after the magnetising force $H$ is reduced to zero**. On the B-H (hysteresis) loop it is the value of $B$ at $H = 0$, called the residual flux density $B_r$. In a DC generator, residual magnetism in the poles is what allows a self-excited generator to build up voltage.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md: Define the following term: (ii) Retentivity
items.answer_md: **Retentivity:** the **ability (property) of a magnetic material to retain magnetism after the magnetising force is removed**. It is measured by the residual flux density $B_r$ when $H$ is reduced to zero from saturation. Hard steel has high retentivity (used for permanent magnets); soft iron and silicon steel have low retentivity (used for transformer and machine cores).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md: Define the following term: (iii) Coercive Force
items.answer_md:
**Coercive force** ($H_c$) is the magnetising force (field intensity) that must be applied in the **reverse direction** to bring the residual flux density of a magnetised material down to **zero**.

- On the B-H (hysteresis) loop it is the intercept on the $H$ axis.
- Unit: ampere-turns per metre (AT/m or A/m).
- High $H_c$ means a hard magnetic material (permanent magnets); low $H_c$ means a soft material (silicon steel for transformer and machine cores).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md: Define the following term: (iv) Magnetic Hysteresis
items.answer_md:
**Magnetic hysteresis** is the lagging of the flux density $B$ behind the magnetising force $H$ when a ferromagnetic material is taken through a cycle of magnetisation.

- Because of it, $B$ does not return to zero when $H$ is removed (residual magnetism), and a reverse $H$ (the coercive force) is needed to remove it; the B-H curve traces a closed **hysteresis loop**.
- The area of the loop is the energy lost per cycle per unit volume as heat (**hysteresis loss**), given by Steinmetz: $P_h = \eta\,B_m^{1.6}\,f\,V$ watts.
- It is kept low in machines and transformers by using silicon steel (narrow loop).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 1 Dr. SC Gupta.pdf
items.question_md: Define the following term: (v) Factors affecting hysteresis loss
items.answer_md:
Hysteresis loss (Steinmetz): $P_h = \eta_h B_m^{1.6} f V$ W. It depends on:
1. **Maximum flux density $B_m$** ($\propto B_m^{1.6}$), set by the applied voltage.
2. **Frequency $f$** (number of magnetisation cycles per second).
3. **Volume $V$** of the magnetic material.
4. **Material**, through the hysteresis coefficient $\eta_h$ (area of the B-H loop); silicon steel has a narrow loop and low loss.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
A 100W resistance is carrying a sinusoidal current given by $3\cos \omega t$. Determine

(i) Instantaneous power taken by resistance
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $R = 100\ \Omega$ (the "100 W" is the resistance value), $i = 3\cos\omega t$ A.

$$p = i^2R = (3\cos\omega t)^2(100) = 900\cos^2\omega t$$
Using $\cos^2\theta = \tfrac12(1 + \cos2\theta)$:
$$\boxed{p = 450 + 450\cos2\omega t\ \text{W}}$$
The power is always positive (a resistor never returns energy), varies between 0 and 900 W, and pulsates at twice the supply frequency.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
A 100W resistance is carrying a sinusoidal current given by $3\cos \omega t$. Determine

(ii) Average power.
items.answer_md:
From part (i): $p = 450 + 450\cos2\omega t$ W for $R = 100\ \Omega$, $i = 3\cos\omega t$ A.

The $\cos2\omega t$ term averages to zero over a cycle, so
$$P_{avg} = \boxed{450\ \text{W}}$$
Check: $I_{rms} = 3/\sqrt2 = 2.121$ A, $P = I_{rms}^2R = 4.5 \times 100 = 450$ W.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md: The current through an 80 mH inductor is $0.1 \sin(400t - 25^\circ)$ Amps. Write the mathematical expression for the voltage across it.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $L = 80$ mH $= 0.08$ H, $i = 0.1\sin(400t - 25^\circ)$ A, so $\omega = 400$ rad/s, $I_m = 0.1$ A.

$$X_L = \omega L = 400 \times 0.08 = 32\ \Omega$$
$$V_m = I_mX_L = 0.1 \times 32 = 3.2\ \text{V}$$
In a pure inductor the voltage **leads** the current by $90^\circ$ (equivalently $v = L\,di/dt = 0.1(400)(0.08)\cos(400t - 25^\circ)$):
$$\boxed{v = 3.2\sin(400t + 65^\circ)\ \text{V}}$$
since $-25^\circ + 90^\circ = 65^\circ$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md: In a four pole ac generator producing alternating current, What will be the span of electrical and mechanical degrees for one revolution of coil?
items.answer_md:
For a $P$-pole machine, $\theta_{elec} = \dfrac{P}{2}\theta_{mech}$.

For one revolution of the coil in a 4-pole generator:
- Mechanical degrees $= $ **360°**
- Electrical degrees $= \dfrac{4}{2}\times360^\circ = $ **720°**, i.e. the emf goes through 2 complete cycles per revolution (one cycle per pair of poles).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
In a delayed full-wave rectified sinusoidal current has an average value equal to half its maximum value. Find the delay angle $\theta$

[Figure: Delayed full-wave rectified sinusoidal current $i$ versus $\theta$ with peak $I_m$; current is zero from $0$ to $\theta$, follows the sine wave from $\theta$ to $\pi$, then zero from $\pi$ to $(\pi+\theta)$, follows the sine wave again up to $2\pi$; axis marks $0$, $\theta$, $\pi$, $(\pi+\theta)$, $2\pi$]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $i = I_m\sin\phi$ for $\theta < \phi < \pi$ (and repeats every $\pi$), zero from 0 to $\theta$. $I_{av} = I_m/2$.

**Average over one period ($\pi$):**
$$I_{av} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\theta}^{\pi}I_m\sin\phi\,d\phi = \frac{I_m}{\pi}\left[-\cos\phi\right]_{\theta}^{\pi} = \frac{I_m}{\pi}(1 + \cos\theta)$$

**Set equal to $I_m/2$:**
$$\frac{1 + \cos\theta}{\pi} = \frac12\Rightarrow\cos\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1 = 0.5708$$
$$\boxed{\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.5708) = 55.2^\circ\ (0.963\ \text{rad})}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
A coil of resistance 100 W and inductance 100 $\mu$H is connected in series with a 100 pF capacitor. The circuit is connected to a 10 V variable frequency source. Calculate (i) the resonant frequency (ii) current at resonance (iii) voltage across L and C at resonance and (iv) Q-factor of the circuit.

Comments on the results so obtained.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $R = 100\ \Omega$ (the "100 W" is the resistance), $L = 100\ \mu$H $= 10^{-4}$ H, $C = 100$ pF $= 10^{-10}$ F, $V = 10$ V.

**(i) Resonant frequency**
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-4}\times10^{-10}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-7}}$$
$$\boxed{f_0 = 1.592\ \text{MHz}}\quad(\omega_0 = 10^7\ \text{rad/s})$$

**(ii) Current at resonance** ($Z = R$)
$$I_0 = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{10}{100} = \boxed{0.1\ \text{A}}$$

**(iii) Voltage across L and C**
$$X_L = X_C = \omega_0L = 10^7 \times 10^{-4} = 1000\ \Omega$$
$$V_L = V_C = I_0X_L = 0.1 \times 1000 = \boxed{100\ \text{V}}$$
(The voltage across the whole coil, including its 100 Ω, is $0.1\sqrt{100^2 + 1000^2} = 100.5$ V.)

**(iv) Q factor**
$$Q = \frac{\omega_0L}{R} = \frac{1000}{100} = \boxed{10}$$

**Comments:**
- At resonance the circuit is purely resistive: minimum impedance (100 Ω), maximum current, unity power factor.
- $V_L$ and $V_C$ are each **10 times** the 10 V supply (voltage magnification = Q); they are equal and opposite so they cancel.
- Hence components must be rated for the magnified voltage, and the circuit selects a narrow band: $BW = f_0/Q = 159.2$ kHz.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2022-23 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md: How will you perform OC test on a 15 KVA, 400 V/11000 V transformer? Why power factor is so poor during this test.
items.answer_md:
**Procedure (OC test on 15 kVA, 400 V/11000 V transformer)**

1. **Connections:** the **400 V (LV) winding** is connected through a wattmeter (current coil in series, pressure coil across), an ammeter and a voltmeter to a 400 V, 50 Hz supply via a variac (autotransformer). The **11 kV (HV) winding is left open** (a voltmeter across it may be used to check the ratio; take care, it is at high voltage).
2. Raise the applied voltage gradually from zero to **rated 400 V** at rated frequency.
3. Record $V_0$ (voltmeter), $I_0$ (ammeter) and $P_0$ (wattmeter).

**Why on the LV side:** rated 400 V is easy and safe to supply, while 11 kV would need a special source; $I_0$ on the LV side is larger and measurable.

**Results:**
- $P_0 = $ iron loss $P_i$ (copper loss $I_0^2R_1$ is negligible).
- $\cos\phi_0 = \dfrac{P_0}{V_0I_0}$, $I_w = I_0\cos\phi_0$, $I_\mu = I_0\sin\phi_0$.
- $R_0 = V_0/I_w$, $X_0 = V_0/I_\mu$ (referred to the LV side).

**Why the power factor is so poor**

With the secondary open, the transformer behaves like a highly inductive coil. $I_0$ is mostly the magnetising component $I_\mu$ (reactive, 90° behind $V_1$, needed to set up the flux), while the working component $I_w$ supplies only the small core loss. Since $I_\mu \gg I_w$, $I_0$ lags $V_1$ by nearly 80-85° and $\cos\phi_0 = I_w/I_0$ is only about **0.1-0.3**. A low-pf wattmeter is therefore used.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain PNP and NPN transistors. Obtain Input/output & transfer characteristics of BJT in CE, CC configurations.
items.answer_md:
### PNP and NPN transistors
- **NPN:** p-type base sandwiched between n-type emitter and collector; electrons are the main carriers; in active mode $V_{BE} > 0$, collector positive; emitter arrow points out.
- **PNP:** n-type base between p-type emitter and collector; holes are the main carriers; all polarities and current directions reversed; emitter arrow points in.
- In both, $I_E = I_B + I_C$, the base is thin and lightly doped, the emitter heavily doped.

### CE configuration
- **Input** ($I_B$ vs $V_{BE}$, $V_{CE}$ constant): diode-like curve, cut-in about 0.7 V (Si); higher $V_{CE}$ shifts it slightly right; $r_i$ about 1 kΩ.
- **Output** ($I_C$ vs $V_{CE}$, $I_B$ constant): steep rise up to $V_{CE} \approx 0.2$ V (saturation), then almost flat (active, $I_C \approx \beta I_B$); the $I_B = 0$ curve gives $I_{CEO}$ (cut-off).
- **Transfer** ($I_C$ vs $I_B$, $V_{CE}$ constant): nearly a straight line, slope $\beta = \Delta I_C/\Delta I_B$ (50 to 300), small intercept $I_{CEO}$.

### CC configuration
- **Input** ($I_B$ vs $V_{CB}$, $V_{CE}$ constant): $I_B$ falls as $V_{CB}$ rises toward $V_{CE}$, because the BE forward bias $V_{BE} = V_{CE} - V_{CB}$ reduces.
- **Output** ($I_E$ vs $V_{CE}$, $I_B$ constant): practically the same shape as the CE output curves, since $I_E \approx I_C$.
- **Transfer** ($I_E$ vs $I_B$): straight line of slope $1 + \beta$ (current gain of CC).
- CC has voltage gain about 1, no phase reversal, highest $r_i$ and lowest $r_o$ (buffer).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the relation of efficiency for full-wave bridge rectifier.
items.answer_md:
**Full-wave bridge rectifier:** in each half cycle two diodes ($D_1, D_3$ in the positive half, $D_2, D_4$ in the negative half) conduct in series with $R_L$, so the load current is unidirectional:
$$i = I_m\sin\theta,\ \ 0 \le \theta \le \pi, \qquad I_m = \frac{V_m}{2r_f + R_L}$$
repeating every $\pi$ ($r_f$ = forward resistance of each diode).

**DC current:**
$$I_{dc} = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{2I_m}{\pi}$$

**RMS current:**
$$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta} = \frac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$$

**Powers:**
$$P_{dc} = I_{dc}^2R_L = \frac{4I_m^2R_L}{\pi^2}, \qquad P_{ac} = I_{rms}^2(2r_f + R_L) = \frac{I_m^2}{2}(2r_f + R_L)$$

**Efficiency:**
$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{R_L}{2r_f + R_L} = \frac{0.812}{1 + 2r_f/R_L}$$

If $2r_f \ll R_L$: $\mathbf{\eta_{max} = 8/\pi^2 = 81.2\%}$, twice that of a half-wave rectifier (40.6%).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
A transistor is connected in common-emitter (CE) configuration in which collector supply is 10 V and voltage drop across resistance $R_C$ connected in the collector circuit is 0.6 V. The value of $R_C = 600\ \Omega$. If $\alpha = 0.95$, determine:

(i) Collector-emitter voltage.

[Figure: NPN transistor in CE configuration; base current $I_B$ supplied from $V_{BB}$; collector current $I_C$ through $R_C = 600\ \Omega$ with 0.6 V drop across it; $V_{CE}$ marked between collector and emitter; emitter current $I_E$; collector supply $V_{CC} = 10$ V]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $V_{CC} = 10$ V, drop across $R_C$: $V_{RC} = I_CR_C = 0.6$ V.

By KVL around the collector circuit:
$$V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_CR_C = 10 - 0.6 = \mathbf{9.4\ V}$$
(Here $I_C = 0.6/600 = 1$ mA.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
A transistor is connected in common-emitter (CE) configuration in which collector supply is 10 V and voltage drop across resistance $R_C$ connected in the collector circuit is 0.6 V. The value of $R_C = 600\ \Omega$. If $\alpha = 0.95$, determine:

(ii) Base current.

[Figure: NPN transistor in CE configuration; base current $I_B$ supplied from $V_{BB}$; collector current $I_C$ through $R_C = 600\ \Omega$ with 0.6 V drop across it; $V_{CE}$ marked between collector and emitter; emitter current $I_E$; collector supply $V_{CC} = 10$ V]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $V_{RC} = 0.6$ V, $R_C = 600\ \Omega$, $\alpha = 0.95$.

**Collector current**
$$I_C = \frac{V_{RC}}{R_C} = \frac{0.6}{600} = 1\ \text{mA}$$

**Current gain**
$$\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{0.95}{0.05} = 19$$

**Base current**
$$I_B = \frac{I_C}{\beta} = \frac{1\ \text{mA}}{19} = \mathbf{52.6\ \mu A}$$
(Check: $I_E = I_C/\alpha = 1.0526$ mA, and $I_E - I_C = 0.0526$ mA $= 52.6\ \mu$A.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is alternating voltage and current. Draw the waveform of AC wave and explain the terms: cycle, amplitude, frequency, time period and RMS value.
items.answer_md:
**Alternating voltage/current:** a voltage or current that periodically reverses direction and continuously changes in magnitude, e.g. $v = V_m\sin\omega t$. (Sketch: a sine wave about the time axis, positive half above, negative half below, $V_m$ marked at the peaks, $T$ marked between successive positive-going zero crossings.)

- **Cycle:** one complete set of positive and negative values (0 to $2\pi$ rad).
- **Amplitude:** the maximum (peak) value, $V_m$ or $I_m$.
- **Time period $T$:** time taken for one cycle (s).
- **Frequency $f$:** number of cycles per second, $f = 1/T$ (Hz); $\omega = 2\pi f$.
- **RMS value:** the steady DC value that produces the same heat in a resistor in the same time; $V_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^Tv^2dt}$, $= V_m/\sqrt2 = 0.707V_m$ for a sine.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain Construction and working principle of DC Machine. Drive the expression for emf when machine is lap and wave connected armature winding.
items.answer_md:
**Construction (main parts)**
1. **Yoke:** outer frame of cast iron/cast steel; gives mechanical support and carries the magnetic flux.
2. **Poles and pole shoes:** laminated steel, bolted to the yoke; carry the field winding, the pole shoe spreads flux over the air gap.
3. **Field winding:** copper coils on the poles; carry current to set up the main flux.
4. **Armature core:** slotted cylinder of laminated silicon steel on the shaft; houses the armature conductors and gives a low-reluctance flux path (laminated to cut eddy loss).
5. **Armature winding:** copper conductors in the slots, lap or wave connected; EMF is induced here.
6. **Commutator:** hard-drawn copper segments insulated by mica; converts the alternating EMF in the armature into DC at the terminals (rectifier action).
7. **Brushes:** carbon/graphite, pressed on the commutator; collect current to the external circuit.

**Working principle**
- **Generator:** based on Faraday's law. When the armature conductors are rotated in the magnetic field they cut flux and a dynamically induced EMF $e = Blv$ appears; direction by Fleming's right-hand rule. The commutator makes the output unidirectional.
- **Motor:** a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force $F = BIl$ (Fleming's left-hand rule); forces on the conductors give a torque that rotates the armature.

**EMF equation**

Let $P$ = poles, $\Phi$ = flux per pole (Wb), $Z$ = total armature conductors, $N$ = speed (rpm), $A$ = number of parallel paths.

- Flux cut by one conductor in one revolution $= P\Phi$ Wb.
- Time for one revolution $= 60/N$ s.
- EMF per conductor $= \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = \dfrac{P\Phi}{60/N} = \dfrac{P\Phi N}{60}$ V.
- Conductors in series in each path $= Z/A$.

$$\boxed{E = \frac{P\Phi N}{60}\cdot\frac{Z}{A} = \frac{P\Phi ZN}{60A}}$$

- **Lap winding:** $A = P$, so $E = \dfrac{\Phi ZN}{60}$
- **Wave winding:** $A = 2$, so $E = \dfrac{P\Phi ZN}{120}$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Obtain the Thevenin and Norton equivalent circuits at terminals *a-b* of the circuit.

[Figure: Left branch: 12 V source (+ at top) in series with a 2 Ω resistor down to the bottom rail (terminal b). From the top of the left branch, a 6 Ω resistor goes down; a 2 Ω resistor runs horizontally along the top to a node leading to terminal a, from which another 6 Ω resistor goes down. The bottoms of the two 6 Ω resistors join and connect through a third 6 Ω resistor in series with a 12 V source (+ at bottom) down to the bottom rail. Right branch: from the top line to terminal a, a 12 V source (+ at top) in series with a 2 Ω resistor down to the bottom rail, terminal b.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading of the circuit:** node L (top of left branch: 12 V, + top, in series with 2 Ω to b); 2 Ω along the top from L to a; 6 Ω from L and 6 Ω from a down to a middle node M; from M, 6 Ω in series with 12 V (+ at bottom) to b; right branch from a: 12 V (+ top) in series with 2 Ω to b.

**Step 1: $V_{th} = V_{ab}$ by nodal analysis** (b = reference).
- Node L: $\dfrac{V_L - 12}{2} + \dfrac{V_L - V_M}{6} + \dfrac{V_L - V_a}{2} = 0$
- Node M: $\dfrac{V_M - V_L}{6} + \dfrac{V_M - V_a}{6} + \dfrac{V_M + 12}{6} = 0$
- Node a: $\dfrac{V_a - V_L}{2} + \dfrac{V_a - V_M}{6} + \dfrac{V_a - 12}{2} = 0$

By symmetry of L and a, $V_L = V_a$ (no current in the top 2 Ω). Then node M gives $3V_M = 2V_a - 12$, and node a gives $\dfrac{V_a - 12}{2} + \dfrac{V_a - V_M}{6} = 0 \Rightarrow 4V_a - V_M = 36$.
Solving: $V_M = 2.4$ V, $V_a = 9.6$ V.
$$V_{th} = \mathbf{9.6\ V}$$

**Step 2: $R_{th}$** (all three 12 V sources shorted). Remaining: L-b 2 Ω, L-a 2 Ω, L-M 6 Ω, a-M 6 Ω, M-b 6 Ω, a-b 2 Ω.
Convert the delta L-a-M (2, 6, 6; sum 14 Ω) to a star with centre S:
$$R_{S,L} = \frac{2\times6}{14} = 0.857\ \Omega,\quad R_{S,a} = \frac{2\times6}{14} = 0.857\ \Omega,\quad R_{S,M} = \frac{6\times6}{14} = 2.571\ \Omega$$
From S to b: via L $= 0.857 + 2 = 2.857\ \Omega$; via M $= 2.571 + 6 = 8.571\ \Omega$; in parallel $= 2.143\ \Omega$.
Path a to b through the network $= 0.857 + 2.143 = 3\ \Omega$, in parallel with the direct 2 Ω:
$$R_{th} = 3 \parallel 2 = \mathbf{1.2\ \Omega}$$

**Step 3: Norton:**
$$I_N = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th}} = \frac{9.6}{1.2} = \mathbf{8\ A},\quad R_N = 1.2\ \Omega$$

**Result:** Thevenin: 9.6 V in series with 1.2 Ω. Norton: 8 A in parallel with 1.2 Ω.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section B.pdf
items.question_md: Define the Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's Laws?
items.answer_md:
**Ohm's law:** at constant temperature (and other physical conditions), the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: $V = IR$, $R$ in ohms.

**Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL):** the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a node is zero; total current entering = total current leaving ($\sum I = 0$).

**Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL):** the algebraic sum of all emfs and voltage drops around any closed loop is zero ($\sum E = \sum IR$).

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section B.pdf
items.question_md: Derive the emf equation of a transformer?
items.answer_md:
Let $N_1$, $N_2$ = primary and secondary turns, $f$ = supply frequency (Hz), $\Phi_m$ = maximum core flux (Wb).

1. A sinusoidal voltage produces a sinusoidal flux: $\Phi = \Phi_m\sin\omega t$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.
2. By Faraday's law, EMF induced in the primary:
$$e_1 = -N_1\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = -N_1\omega\Phi_m\cos\omega t = N_1\omega\Phi_m\sin(\omega t - 90^\circ)$$
So $e_1$ lags the flux by 90°, with maximum value
$$E_{1,max} = 2\pi fN_1\Phi_m$$
3. RMS value $= E_{max}/\sqrt2$:
$$E_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt2}fN_1\Phi_m = 4.44fN_1\Phi_m$$
4. Similarly for the secondary (same flux links it):

$$\boxed{E_1 = 4.44fN_1\Phi_m, \qquad E_2 = 4.44fN_2\Phi_m}$$

With $\Phi_m = B_mA$: $E = 4.44fNB_mA$. Also $\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = K$ (transformation ratio) and EMF per turn is the same on both sides.

items.question_md:
Determine the equivalent resistance between the terminals A and B as shown below figure?

[Figure: Resistor network between terminals A and B. From terminal B a 2 Ω resistor leads to a top node, followed by a 15 Ω resistor to the top-right corner. The right side has a 10 Ω resistor and then another 10 Ω resistor going down. Terminal A connects to an 8 Ω resistor on the left side, followed by a 20 Ω resistor below it. The bottom side has a 30 Ω resistor and a 40 Ω resistor. A horizontal wire joins the left-middle node to the right-middle node. A vertical wire runs from the top node after the 2 Ω resistor to the bottom node between the 30 Ω and 40 Ω resistors. The two wires cross without connecting (shown by a hop).]
items.answer_md:
**Key observation:** the two wires cross without connecting (hop), so there are two separate nodes: H (horizontal wire, joining the middle-left and middle-right nodes) and V (vertical wire, joining the top node after 2 Ω to the bottom node between 30 Ω and 40 Ω).

**Step 1: Paths between H and V.**
- Upper right: V, 15 Ω, top-right corner, 10 Ω, H: $15 + 10 = 25\ \Omega$
- Lower right: H, 10 Ω, bottom-right corner, 40 Ω, V: $10 + 40 = 50\ \Omega$
- Lower left: H, 20 Ω, bottom-left corner, 30 Ω, V: $20 + 30 = 50\ \Omega$

**Step 2: Parallel combination.**
$$R_{HV} = 25 \parallel 50 \parallel 50 = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{25} + \frac{1}{50} + \frac{1}{50}} = 12.5\ \Omega$$

**Step 3: Series with the terminal resistors.** A, 8 Ω, H, $R_{HV}$, V, 2 Ω, B:
$$R_{AB} = 8 + 12.5 + 2 = \mathbf{22.5\ \Omega}$$

items.question_md:
Use Thevenin's theorem to find the power delivered to 1 ohm resistor in below figure?

[Figure: Circuit with a 20 V source on the left. A 6 Ω resistor runs along the top branch. Two middle branches are present. The left middle branch has a 2 Ω resistor above, then a 5 Ω resistor in series with a 20 V source below. The right branch has a 3 Ω resistor above and a 4 Ω resistor below. A 1 Ω resistor connects the junction between the 2 Ω and 5 Ω resistors to the junction between the 3 Ω and 4 Ω resistors. The bottom is a common return line.]
items.answer_md:
**Reading:** 20 V source (+ top) and 6 Ω feed node P. Branch 1 from P: 2 Ω to node X, 5 Ω to the + of a 20 V source (+ top) whose − is on the bottom rail. Branch 2 from P: 3 Ω to node Z, 4 Ω to the bottom rail. The 1 Ω joins X and Z.

**Step 1: Remove the 1 Ω.**

**Step 2: $V_{th} = V_X - V_Z$.** KCL at P (branch 1 is 7 Ω to a 20 V point, branch 2 is 7 Ω to ground):
$$\frac{V_P - 20}{6} + \frac{V_P - 20}{7} + \frac{V_P}{7} = 0 \Rightarrow V_P = 13.68\ \text{V}$$
Branch 1 current (P to 20 V): $\dfrac{13.68 - 20}{7} = -0.902$ A, so $V_X = V_P - 2(-0.902) = 15.49$ V.
Branch 2 current: $\dfrac{13.68}{7} = 1.955$ A, so $V_Z = 4 \times 1.955 = 7.82$ V.
$$V_{th} = 15.49 - 7.82 = 7.67\ \text{V}\ (\text{X positive})$$

**Step 3: $R_{th}$** (both 20 V sources shorted). P now has 6 Ω, X has 5 Ω and Z has 4 Ω to ground, so the network between X and Z is a bridge. Convert the star at P (arms 2 Ω to X, 3 Ω to Z, 6 Ω to ground) into a delta:
$$R_{XZ} = 2 + 3 + \frac{2\cdot3}{6} = 6\ \Omega,\quad R_{XG} = 2 + 6 + \frac{2\cdot6}{3} = 12\ \Omega,\quad R_{ZG} = 3 + 6 + \frac{3\cdot6}{2} = 18\ \Omega$$
$$R_{th} = R_{XZ} \parallel \big[(12 \parallel 5) + (18 \parallel 4)\big] = 6 \parallel (3.529 + 3.273) = 6 \parallel 6.802 = 3.188\ \Omega$$

**Step 4: Current and power in 1 Ω.**
$$I = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + 1} = \frac{7.67}{4.188} = 1.831\ \text{A}\ (\text{X to Z})$$
$$P = I^2 R = 1.831^2 \times 1 = \mathbf{3.35\ W}$$

(Polarity of the middle 20 V source is taken + at top; the method is unchanged for the other polarity.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section B.pdf
items.question_md: A 200 kVA rated transformer has an iron loss of 1 kW and a half-load copper loss of 1.5 kW and it is operating at 0.85 power factor. Determine the transformer efficiencies at 50 % and 75 % of full load and also find the maximum efficiency of transformer?
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $S = 200$ kVA, $P_i = 1$ kW, copper loss at half load $= 1.5$ kW, pf $= 0.85$.

Copper loss varies as the square of load:
$$P_{cu,fl} = \frac{1.5}{(0.5)^2} = 6\ \text{kW}$$

**Efficiency formula:** $\eta = \dfrac{xS\cos\phi}{xS\cos\phi + P_i + x^2P_{cu,fl}}\times 100$

**At 50% load:**
$$\text{Output} = 0.5 \times 200 \times 0.85 = 85\ \text{kW}, \quad \text{losses} = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5\ \text{kW}$$
$$\eta_{50} = \frac{85}{87.5}\times 100 = \mathbf{97.14\%}$$

**At 75% load:**
$$\text{Output} = 0.75 \times 200 \times 0.85 = 127.5\ \text{kW}, \quad P_{cu} = 0.75^2 \times 6 = 3.375\ \text{kW}$$
$$\eta_{75} = \frac{127.5}{127.5 + 1 + 3.375}\times 100 = \frac{127.5}{131.875}\times 100 = \mathbf{96.68\%}$$

**Maximum efficiency:** occurs when copper loss = iron loss:
$$x = \sqrt{\frac{P_i}{P_{cu,fl}}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{6}} = 0.4082 \ \Rightarrow\ \text{load} = 0.4082 \times 200 = 81.65\ \text{kVA}$$
$$\text{Output} = 81.65 \times 0.85 = 69.40\ \text{kW}, \quad \text{losses} = 1 + 1 = 2\ \text{kW}$$
$$\eta_{max} = \frac{69.40}{71.40}\times 100$$
$$\boxed{\eta_{max} \approx 97.20\%\ \text{at } 0.85 \text{ pf, at } 81.65\ \text{kVA}}$$

items.question_md:
Determine the Power loss in 3 ohms resistor by applying Thevenin's theorem in the following network.

[Figure: Circuit with a 10 V source on the left branch, connected through a 2 Ω series resistor on the top wire to a node; from this node a vertical branch of 5 Ω in series with a 12 V source goes to the bottom wire; a 3 Ω resistor is connected in parallel between top and bottom wires; on the right, a 1 Ω resistor on the top wire connects to a 20 V source in the right branch going to the bottom wire.]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** top node T is fed by 10 V through 2 Ω, by 12 V through 5 Ω and by 20 V through 1 Ω (all + at top); the 3 Ω is across T and the bottom rail.

**Step 1: Remove the 3 Ω.** $V_{th} = V_T$.

**Step 2: $V_{th}$** (KCL at T):
$$\frac{V_T - 10}{2} + \frac{V_T - 12}{5} + \frac{V_T - 20}{1} = 0$$
$$V_T = \frac{5 + 2.4 + 20}{0.5 + 0.2 + 1} = \frac{27.4}{1.7} = 16.12\ \text{V}$$

**Step 3: $R_{th}$** (sources shorted):
$$R_{th} = 2 \parallel 5 \parallel 1 = \frac{1}{1.7} = 0.588\ \Omega$$

**Step 4: Current and power loss in 3 Ω:**
$$I = \frac{16.12}{0.588 + 3} = \frac{16.12}{3.588} = 4.49\ \text{A}$$
$$P = I^2 R = 4.49^2 \times 3 = \mathbf{60.5\ W}$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section D.pdf
items.question_md:
Using Mesh analysis, determine the currents $I_X$ and $I_Y$ in the network as shown in the Fig.

[Figure: Two-mesh circuit. Left branch: 12 V source (+ at top). Top wire: 5 Ω resistor from the left branch to the middle node, then 6 Ω resistor to the right branch. Middle vertical branch: 2 Ω resistor. Right branch: 6 V source (+ at top). Bottom wire of right mesh: 4 Ω resistor. A 3 A current source is connected across the top, from the right side to the left side (arrow pointing left), in parallel with the 5 Ω and 6 Ω path. Mesh currents $I_X$ (left mesh) and $I_Y$ (right mesh) shown clockwise.]
items.answer_md:
**Set-up:** $I_X$ (left mesh), $I_Y$ (right mesh), clockwise. The 3 A source across the top forms a third mesh (above the 5 Ω–6 Ω path) whose current is fixed: the source drives 3 A right-to-left along the top, so that mesh current is 3 A anticlockwise. Hence it flows **left to right** through 5 Ω and 6 Ω. Branch currents (left to right):
$$I_{5\Omega} = I_X + 3,\qquad I_{6\Omega} = I_Y + 3,\qquad I_{2\Omega}\ (\text{down}) = I_X - I_Y$$

**Mesh X:** rise of 12 V (going up through the 12 V source, + at top) equals the drops:
$$12 = 5(I_X + 3) + 2(I_X - I_Y)\ \Rightarrow\ 7I_X - 2I_Y = -3$$

**Mesh Y:** going clockwise, the 6 V source (+ at top) is a drop:
$$0 = 6(I_Y + 3) + 6 + 4I_Y + 2(I_Y - I_X)\ \Rightarrow\ -2I_X + 12I_Y = -24$$

**Solving:**
$$\Delta = 7(12) - (-2)(-2) = 80$$
$$I_X = \frac{(-3)(12) - (-2)(-24)}{80} = \frac{-84}{80} = \mathbf{-1.05\ A},\qquad I_Y = \frac{7(-24) - (-2)(-3)}{80} = \frac{-174}{80} = \mathbf{-2.175\ A}$$
The minus signs mean both mesh currents actually flow **anticlockwise**.

**Branch currents:** 5 Ω: 1.95 A; 6 Ω: 0.825 A (both left to right); 2 Ω: 1.125 A downward.
Check: $5(1.95) + 2(1.125) = 12$ V ✓.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section D.pdf
items.question_md: Two impedances consist of (resistance of 15 ohm and series connected inductance of 0.04 H) and (resistance of 10 ohms, inductance of 0.1 H and a capacitance of 100 μF all in series) are connected in series and are connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz a.c. sources. Find (i) current drawn (ii) voltage across each impedance, (iii) Individual and total power factor.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $V = 230$ V, $f = 50$ Hz, $\omega = 314.16$ rad/s.

**Impedances**
- $Z_1$: $R_1 = 15\ \Omega$, $X_{L1} = 314.16 \times 0.04 = 12.566\ \Omega$; $\bar Z_1 = 15 + j12.566 = 19.568\angle39.96^\circ\ \Omega$
- $Z_2$: $R_2 = 10\ \Omega$, $X_{L2} = 314.16\times0.1 = 31.416\ \Omega$, $X_{C2} = \dfrac{1}{314.16\times100\times10^{-6}} = 31.831\ \Omega$; $\bar Z_2 = 10 - j0.415 = 10.009\angle{-2.38^\circ}\ \Omega$
- Total: $\bar Z = 25 + j12.151 = 27.797\angle25.92^\circ\ \Omega$

**(i) Current**
$$I = \frac{230}{27.797} = \mathbf{8.274\ A},\ \text{lagging } V \text{ by } 25.92^\circ$$

**(ii) Voltage across each impedance**
- $V_1 = IZ_1 = 8.274 \times 19.568 = $ **161.9 V**
- $V_2 = IZ_2 = 8.274\times10.009 = $ **82.8 V**

(They add as phasors to 230 V, not arithmetically.)

**(iii) Power factors**
- $\cos\phi_1 = R_1/Z_1 = 15/19.568 = $ **0.767 lagging**
- $\cos\phi_2 = R_2/Z_2 = 10/10.009 = $ **0.999 leading** (since $X_{C2} > X_{L2}$)
- Total: $\cos\phi = R/Z = 25/27.797 = $ **0.899 lagging**

Power drawn: $P = I^2R = 8.274^2 \times 25 = 1711.6$ W.

items.question_md:
The following test results were obtained on a 20 kVA, 2200/220 V, 50 Hz single phase transformer.

| Test | Voltage | Current | Power |
|---|---|---|---|
| OC Test (LV side) | 220 V | 1.1 A | 125 W |
| SC Test (HV side) | 52.7 V | 8.4 A | 287 W |

Determine parameter of the equivalent circuit diagram and draw it. Calculate voltage regulation of the transformer for full load 0.85 pf lagging.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 20 kVA, 2200/220 V, 50 Hz. OC (LV): 220 V, 1.1 A, 125 W. SC (HV): 52.7 V, 8.4 A, 287 W. $K^2 = (2200/220)^2 = 100$.

**Shunt branch (OC test, LV side):**
$$\cos\phi_0 = \frac{125}{220 \times 1.1} = 0.5165, \quad \sin\phi_0 = 0.8563$$
$$I_w = 1.1 \times 0.5165 = 0.568\ \text{A}, \quad I_\mu = 1.1 \times 0.8563 = 0.942\ \text{A}$$
$$R_0 = \frac{220}{0.568} = 387.2\ \Omega, \quad X_0 = \frac{220}{0.942} = 233.6\ \Omega \quad\text{(LV)}$$
Referred to HV: $R_0 = 38\,720\ \Omega$, $X_0 = 23\,357\ \Omega$.

**Series branch (SC test, HV side):**
$$Z_{01} = \frac{52.7}{8.4} = 6.274\ \Omega, \quad R_{01} = \frac{287}{8.4^2} = 4.067\ \Omega, \quad X_{01} = \sqrt{6.274^2 - 4.067^2} = 4.777\ \Omega$$
Referred to LV: $R_{02} = 0.0407\ \Omega$, $X_{02} = 0.0478\ \Omega$.

**Equivalent circuit (referred to HV):** input terminals at 2200 V, shunt branch $R_0 = 38.72\ \text{k}\Omega \parallel X_0 = 23.36\ \text{k}\Omega$ across them, then series $R_{01} = 4.067\ \Omega$ and $X_{01} = 4.777\ \Omega$ to the load side (load voltage $V_2' = KV_2$).

**Voltage regulation at full load, 0.85 pf lagging**
$$I_1 = \frac{20000}{2200} = 9.091\ \text{A}, \quad \cos\phi = 0.85,\ \sin\phi = 0.5268$$
$$\%R = \frac{I_1(R_{01}\cos\phi + X_{01}\sin\phi)}{V_1}\times 100 = \frac{9.091(4.067 \times 0.85 + 4.777 \times 0.5268)}{2200}\times 100$$
$$= \frac{54.31}{2200}\times 100$$
$$\boxed{\%R \approx 2.47\%}$$

(Note: SC current 8.4 A is below rated 9.09 A; the parameters are still valid, and rated current is used for regulation.)

items.question_md:
Find $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ in the network, using loop-current method.

[Figure: Three-loop network with mesh currents $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$ (left to right). Left branch: 10 V source. Top branch, left to right: 10 Ω resistor, then a 40 V battery in series with a 20 Ω resistor, then a 10 Ω resistor. Middle shunt branch between loops 1 and 2: 20 Ω resistor. Shunt branch between loops 2 and 3: 10 V source in series with a 10 Ω resistor. Right branch: 50 V source.]
items.answer_md:
**Assumed polarities** (the figure's polarity marks decide the signs; redo the signs if they differ): 10 V left source + at top; 40 V battery + on its right side; 10 V in the shunt between loops 2 and 3 + at top; 50 V right source + at top. Mesh currents $I_1, I_2, I_3$ clockwise.

**Self and mutual resistances**
- Loop 1: 10 + 20 = 30 Ω; shares 20 Ω with loop 2.
- Loop 2: 20 + 20 + 10 = 50 Ω; shares 20 Ω with loop 1 and 10 Ω with loop 3.
- Loop 3: 10 + 10 = 20 Ω; shares 10 Ω with loop 2.

**Mesh equations** ($\sum$ emf aiding the mesh current $= \sum$ drops):
- Loop 1: $30I_1 - 20I_2 = 10$
- Loop 2: $-20I_1 + 50I_2 - 10I_3 = 40 - 10 = 30$
- Loop 3: $-10I_2 + 20I_3 = 10 - 50 = -40$

**Matrix form and solution**
$$\begin{bmatrix}30 & -20 & 0\\ -20 & 50 & -10\\ 0 & -10 & 20\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I_1\\I_2\\I_3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}10\\30\\-40\end{bmatrix}$$
$\Delta = 30(1000 - 100) + 20(-400) = 19000$
$$I_1 = \frac{13000}{19000} = \mathbf{0.684\ A},\quad I_2 = \frac{10000}{19000} = \mathbf{0.526\ A},\quad I_3 = \frac{-33000}{19000} = \mathbf{-1.737\ A}$$
$I_3$ is negative: it flows anticlockwise. Branch currents: 20 Ω shunt $I_1 - I_2 = 0.158$ A downward; 10 Ω shunt $I_2 - I_3 = 2.263$ A downward.

Check loop 1: $30(0.684) - 20(0.526) = 10.0$ ✓.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md: Why average power consumed in pure capacitive circuit is zero? How does capacitive reactance vary with frequency?
items.answer_md:
**Average power in a pure capacitor is zero**

Let $v = V_m\sin\omega t$. Then $i = C\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \omega CV_m\cos\omega t = I_m\sin(\omega t + 90^\circ)$, i.e. the current leads by $90^\circ$.

$$p = vi = V_mI_m\sin\omega t\cos\omega t = \frac{V_mI_m}{2}\sin2\omega t$$
$$P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{V_mI_m}{2}\sin2\omega t\,d(\omega t) = 0$$
Physically, in the quarter cycle when the voltage rises the capacitor **stores** energy $\tfrac12CV_m^2$ in its electric field (p positive); in the next quarter the voltage falls and the same energy is **returned** to the source (p negative). Net energy consumed per cycle is zero. Equivalently $P = VI\cos90^\circ = 0$.

**Variation of $X_C$ with frequency**
$$X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi fC}\ \Omega$$
$X_C$ is **inversely proportional** to frequency: the graph of $X_C$ against $f$ is a rectangular hyperbola. At $f = 0$ (DC) $X_C \to \infty$ (capacitor blocks DC, acts as an open circuit); as $f \to \infty$, $X_C \to 0$ (acts as a short circuit).

items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with capacitor of capacitance 12 μF.

Estimate:

(i) The frequency at which resonance will occur.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** coil $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$; $C = 12\ \mu$F $= 12\times10^{-6}$ F.

$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{0.64 \times 12\times10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{7.68\times10^{-6}}}$$
$$\boxed{f_0 = 57.43\ \text{Hz}}\quad(\omega_0 = 360.84\ \text{rad/s})$$

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with capacitor of capacitance 12 μF.

Estimate:

(ii) The voltage across the coil and capacitor, respectively and also the supply voltage when a current of 1.5 A at the resonant frequency is flowing.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$, $C = 12\ \mu$F, $I = 1.5$ A at $f_0 = 57.43$ Hz ($\omega_0 = 360.84$ rad/s).

**Reactances at resonance:**
$$X_L = \omega_0L = 360.84 \times 0.64 = 230.94\ \Omega,\qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega_0C} = 230.94\ \Omega$$

**Voltage across the coil** (coil has $R$ and $L$):
$$Z_{coil} = \sqrt{40^2 + 230.94^2} = 234.38\ \Omega$$
$$V_{coil} = IZ_{coil} = 1.5 \times 234.38 = \boxed{351.6\ \text{V}}$$

**Voltage across the capacitor:**
$$V_C = IX_C = 1.5 \times 230.94 = \boxed{346.4\ \text{V}}$$

**Supply voltage:** at resonance $Z = R$
$$V = IR = 1.5 \times 40 = \boxed{60\ \text{V}}$$

The coil and capacitor voltages are each nearly 6 times the supply voltage ($Q = 230.94/40 = 5.77$), because their reactive parts cancel.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
A coil of inductance 0.64 H and resistance 40 Ω is connected in series with capacitor of capacitance 12 μF.

Estimate:

(iii) The supply voltage with a current of 1.5 A flowing at a frequency of 50 Hz.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $L = 0.64$ H, $R = 40\ \Omega$, $C = 12\ \mu$F, $I = 1.5$ A, $f = 50$ Hz.

**Reactances:**
$$X_L = 2\pi(50)(0.64) = 201.06\ \Omega,\qquad X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi(50)(12\times10^{-6})} = 265.26\ \Omega$$
$$X_L - X_C = -64.20\ \Omega\ \text{(net capacitive)}$$
**Impedance:**
$$Z = \sqrt{40^2 + 64.20^2} = 75.64\ \Omega$$
**Supply voltage:**
$$V = IZ = 1.5 \times 75.64 = \boxed{113.5\ \text{V}}$$
The circuit is below its resonant frequency (57.43 Hz), so it is capacitive: power factor $= 40/75.64 = 0.529$ leading ($\phi = 58.07^\circ$). Compare 60 V needed at resonance.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
Perform the open circuit test on 230/115 V 15 kVA transformer and answer the following in brief-

(i) What is the purpose of this test?
items.answer_md:
**Purpose of the open-circuit (no-load) test:**
1. To measure the **iron (core) loss** $P_i$ of the transformer at rated voltage; this is constant at all loads.
2. To find the **no-load current** $I_0$ and its components $I_w = I_0\cos\phi_0$ and $I_\mu = I_0\sin\phi_0$.
3. To determine the **shunt branch parameters** $R_0 = V_0/I_w$ and $X_0 = V_0/I_\mu$ of the equivalent circuit.
4. (With a voltmeter on the open HV side) to check the **transformation ratio**.

These are needed to predict efficiency and to draw the equivalent circuit without loading the transformer.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
Perform the open circuit test on 230/115 V 15 kVA transformer and answer the following in brief-

(ii) Why the power factor becomes low during the test?
items.answer_md:
On open circuit the transformer draws only the no-load current $I_0$, which is mostly **magnetising current** $I_\mu$ (reactive, needed to set up the flux) and only a small **working component** $I_w$ (to supply the small core loss).

Since $I_\mu \gg I_w$, $I_0$ lags $V_1$ by nearly 90° (typically 75-85°), so
$$\cos\phi_0 = \frac{P_0}{V_0I_0} = \frac{I_w}{I_0}$$
is very low, typically **0.1 to 0.3 lagging**. (A low-pf wattmeter is therefore used in this test.)

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
Perform the open circuit test on 230/115 V 15 kVA transformer and answer the following in brief-

(iii) How much voltage you need to apply & why?
items.answer_md:
Apply **rated voltage, 115 V at rated frequency, to the LV (115 V) side** with the 230 V side open.

**Why:**
- Iron loss depends on the maximum flux density, $\Phi_m = V/(4.44fN)$; only at rated voltage and frequency is the flux, and therefore the core loss measured, equal to that in normal operation.
- 115 V is easier and safer to obtain and measure than 230 V, and the no-load current on the LV side ($I_0$ is about 2-5% of rated) is larger and easier to read on the ammeter.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.question_md:
Perform the open circuit test on 230/115 V 15 kVA transformer and answer the following in brief-

(iv) What will happen if you apply only 100 V to perform this test?
items.answer_md:
The OC test is normally done on the 115 V (LV) side at **rated voltage 115 V**. Applying only 100 V (about 87% of rated):

- Flux $\Phi_m = \dfrac{V}{4.44fN}$ falls in proportion, so $B_m$ is below the rated value.
- Core loss falls ($P_h \propto B_m^{1.6}$, $P_e \propto B_m^2$), so the wattmeter reads **less than the actual rated iron loss**.
- The no-load current and the computed $R_0$, $X_0$ will not represent rated operation, so efficiency calculated from this test will be **wrong (overestimated)**.

(If 100 V were applied to the 230 V side, the flux would be under half the rated value and the readings would be even more meaningless.) Hence the test must be done at rated voltage and frequency.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term Previous Year Questions/Mid Term 2024 Sem 2 Section E.pdf
items.topic: Transformer phasor diagrams and equivalent circuit
items.question_md: A 230 V/115 V single-phase transformer takes a no-load current of 2 A at a power factor of 0.2 lagging with low voltage winding kept open. If the low voltage winding is now loaded to take a current of 15 A at 0.8 power factor lagging find the current taken by high voltage winding. Draw the vector diagram showing all angles and no load current.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** 230/115 V, so $K = N_2/N_1 = 115/230 = 0.5$. No load: $I_0 = 2$ A at $\cos\phi_0 = 0.2$ lag. Load (LV): $I_2 = 15$ A at $\cos\phi_2 = 0.8$ lag.

**To find:** HV current $I_1$.

**Angles:**
$$\phi_0 = \cos^{-1}0.2 = 78.46^\circ, \qquad \phi_2 = \cos^{-1}0.8 = 36.87^\circ$$

**Load component of primary current:**
$$I_2' = KI_2 = 0.5 \times 15 = 7.5\ \text{A at } 36.87^\circ \text{ lag (w.r.t. } V_1)$$

**Resolve with $V_1$ as reference** ($\bar I_1 = \bar I_0 + \bar I_2'$):

| | Horizontal ($\cos$) | Vertical ($-\sin$) |
|---|---|---|
| $I_0$ | $2 \times 0.2 = 0.4$ | $-2 \times 0.9798 = -1.960$ |
| $I_2'$ | $7.5 \times 0.8 = 6.0$ | $-7.5 \times 0.6 = -4.5$ |
| $I_1$ | $6.4$ | $-6.460$ |

$$I_1 = \sqrt{6.4^2 + 6.460^2}$$
$$\boxed{I_1 \approx 9.09\ \text{A}}, \quad \phi_1 = \tan^{-1}\frac{6.460}{6.4} = 45.27^\circ \text{ lag},\ \cos\phi_1 = 0.704$$

**Vector diagram (with $V_1$ as reference, horizontal):**
- $\Phi$ lags $V_1$ by 90° (vertically down); $E_1$ opposite $V_1$; $E_2$ in phase with $E_1$ (half its length).
- $I_0 = 2$ A drawn 78.46° behind $V_1$ (11.54° ahead of $\Phi$).
- $I_2 = 15$ A drawn 36.87° behind $V_2$; $I_2' = 7.5$ A drawn 36.87° behind $V_1$ (antiphase to $I_2$ as reflected).
- $I_1 = 9.09$ A is the diagonal of the parallelogram of $I_0$ and $I_2'$, at 45.27° behind $V_1$.

items.path: library/archive/EE1108/Mid Term/Mid Term Section F Sem 1 2025-26 .pdf
items.question_md: Define active, reactive and apparent power in a single-phase AC circuit and derive their relation using Power Triangle.
items.answer_md:
Let $v = V_m\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, with RMS values $V$, $I$.

**Definitions**
- **Active (real, true) power** $P$: the average power actually consumed (converted to heat or work), $P = VI\cos\phi$, unit **W**.
- **Reactive power** $Q$: the power that oscillates between the source and the L or C fields, doing no net work, $Q = VI\sin\phi$, unit **VAR**.
- **Apparent power** $S$: the product of RMS voltage and current, $S = VI$, unit **VA**.

**Derivation via power triangle**

Resolve the current phasor $I$ (lagging $V$ by $\phi$) into:
- an **active component** $I\cos\phi$, in phase with $V$
- a **reactive component** $I\sin\phi$, in quadrature ($90^\circ$) with $V$

Multiply each side of this current triangle by $V$:
- base $VI\cos\phi = P$
- perpendicular $VI\sin\phi = Q$
- hypotenuse $VI = S$

This right-angled triangle is the **power triangle**, with angle $\phi$ between $P$ and $S$. Hence
$$\boxed{S^2 = P^2 + Q^2},\qquad \cos\phi = \frac{P}{S},\qquad \tan\phi = \frac{Q}{P}$$
In complex form $\bar S = P + jQ$ (Q positive for a lagging, inductive load). The power triangle is also the impedance triangle $(R, X, Z)$ multiplied by $I^2$: $P = I^2R$, $Q = I^2X$, $S = I^2Z$.
